articles.title: The week in photos: October 24-30, 2026
articles.summary: A recap of news, sports, lifestyle, entertainment, and human interest images from the Philippines and around the globe

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — On October 25, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term. Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century, defeated Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. The senator had finished first in the election’s first round and hoped to revive his father’s far-right movement.

In Serbia, tens of thousands of people took to the streets across the country to celebrate when longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat on October 25, in a historic poll that capped two years of peaceful anti-government protests. By unseating Vucic, Serbia’s student protest movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of.

In Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu looked set to remain the country’s caretaker prime minister after unexpectedly strong backing among Jewish voters left his opponents little apparent prospect of unseating him. With nearly 86% of votes tallied on October 28, Netanyahu’s bloc of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties is projected win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, well ahead of the 48 for rival Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc.

Meanwhile, during the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) in Cebu on October 28, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. emphasized the importance of unity among ASEAN members despite differing ties with China, advocating for peaceful resolution of disputes, particularly in the South China Sea.

ADMM and the ADMM-Plus is an annual gathering of defense ministers from Southeast Asia and “plus countries” or ADMM dialogue partners Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia, and the United States. Chinese Defense Minister Dong Jun skips the ADMM-Plus meeting, as bilateral ties between Manila and Beijing hit their tensest note yet.

articles.title: The cursed cruise: how the dream of never-ending luxury at sea became a nightmare
articles.summary:
The MV Odyssey was billed as the ultimate escape from Donald Trump. Instead, the oil shock caused by his war has left passengers unceremoniously dumped in Cambodia

The idea was a…
articles.byline: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok, Daniel Boffey in London and Adeshola Ore in Melbourne

blocks.text: The idea was a never-ending retirement at sea, a continuous voyage around the globe. The promise to the passengers of the MV Odyssey cruise ship – many approaching the autumn of their lives – was that on the open seas they could cut loose from the troubles of the world. But the world had other ideas.
The end came in an announcement as stark as it was brief: they had seven hours to get off. They were going no further than Cambodia.

The Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, had first set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024 with an explicit offer: Donald Trump had been re-elected to the White House, and this was a way for those ill-disposed to the president to enjoy a four-year “skip forward”.

blocks.caption: Passengers disembark from the Odyssey at Sihanoukville port in Cambodia. Photograph: Kith Serey/EPA

blocks.text: For $319,998, a couple seeking such an escape could head off to the high seas for the length of a presidential term and come back from their journey to nowhere when the danger had passed – or not. For those who had simply had enough, there was a permanent residency option for a few hundred thousand more. Depending on the package, there were also monthly fees on top, which covered food, drinks, wifi, wellness programmes and room cleaning. They would have access to a pool, a pickleball court, a theatre, several bars and a gym. Exotic port destinations would be visited along the way.

It was by no means cheap – but the Odyssey was quite accurately billed as the “affordable” option for those interested in such a cocoon. The pioneer in the world of “residential ships”, a vessel called MS The World, offered apartments that typically ranged from $2m to $15m, with the pampered passengers getting to choose where it would go. For that experience, there was a waiting list.

The Odyssey was not in that league. Rather than built as a residential ship, it had previously been a traditional cruise liner named MS Braemar. Under that name, it had been turned away from several ports in the Caribbean during the pandemic when its passengers became ill. Cuba finally allowed it to dock, but the vessel never went into service as MS Braemar again. It was sold off by Fred Olsen cruises and adapted by its new owners. Villa Vie described the three-decade-old restructured vessel as “an intimate residential cruise ship offering a new way to live”.

blocks.caption: Passengers onboard the then-MS Braemar wait to disembark in Mariel, Cuba, in March 2020. Photograph: Adalberto Roque/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: At 642ft (196 metres) long, it was a relatively small ship, but at such prices, and with the world being held firmly at bay, what could go wrong? Neither the more than 200 passengers on the Odyssey nor its cruise operator foresaw the consequences of Trump’s war in Iran. The reality was, there was no escaping the US president.

On Tuesday, Villa Vie Residences issued a statement. It had run out of money owing to the soaring price of oil. Monthly fuel costs per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, placing it “under unsustainable financial pressure”, it announced.

“Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said, explaining the slow death of its business model. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.”

blocks.caption: The Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship leaves Belfast. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA

blocks.text: The Odyssey’s passengers were told to pack up their belongings before being transported on buses into the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand. “We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalisation alternatives over the next 60 days,” the company said.

“People were shell-shocked, numb, crying,” said one passenger, Kit Cassingham from the US, who spent two years on the ship with her husband, Randy. They had made their cabin into a home, putting down their own rugs and pictures on the wall. “People were angry. They were hysterical. They were sad … Disbelief,” she added. “I mean, that whole gamut of, what is it, the five stages of grief.”

Most of the passengers on the Odyssey were Americans, travelling with an international group of 156 crew members, including a ship’s doctor and two nurses. Many of the passengers were retired or digital nomads. One woman, Holly Hennessy, had been living happily with her cat, Captain, since the ship set sail two years ago.

blocks.caption: Holly Hennessy with her Siamese cat, Captain, in Belfast. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA

blocks.text: One couple, Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin, who said they had bought a cabin with a 15-year guarantee, had been documenting their life at sea on YouTube, including the lead-up to the fateful announcement. The signs of financial distress had been apparent for weeks, they said.
“I’m Mr Super Positive, and I’ve felt really drained the last two months,” Bodin recounted in a video.

Footage from inside the ship’s lounge on the final night showed residents drinking, as rumours spread that their voyage might be over. Cruise ship staff had requested each passenger contribute $1,800 to ensure the ship had funds to travel to Bangkok.

The next day, the couple posted an update showing the inside of their cabin as a voice on the loudspeaker said the ship’s operator had “unfortunately” been “unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations”. An email was sent requesting that everyone disembark by 2pm.
“We knew the worst-case scenarios, but we didn’t think it would come to reality, which it did,” said Rina Cavazza, a pilates instructor from Brisbane, Australia.

blocks.caption: Rina Cavazza’s cabin on the Villa Vie Odyssey. Photograph: supplied

blocks.text: Another passenger, Sherrie Cornett, wrote on Facebook that they were “dropped unceremoniously in the middle of town, left to our own devices”.

The company has not provided financial aid, passengers said, or even supplied a list of hotels in Cambodia. It later offered tickets for a charter flight to the US, although many passengers had already left. The company has been contacted for comment.

Kit and Randy Cassingham, now in a hotel in Cambodia, reflected on how life changed on the ship once the Iran war began, with ominous signs that the company was running out of money. The food quality began to deteriorate, and there was less of it; there were fewer excursions on shore, they said.

blocks.caption: Randy and Kit Cassingham: ‘Live life while you can because you don’t know how the adventure will turn out.’ Photograph: Tang Chhin Sothy/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “I realised as soon as the strait of Hormuz incident came along, the energy of the ship changed,” Kit said. “I think it was because the ship management realised how much more this was going to cost. And then they were starting to do cutbacks that we weren’t aware of yet.”

Far from being a haven, the ship became a microcosm for the global economic turmoil. “I watched the world, and I don’t even pay attention to the news, but I’ve watched it just kind of crumble and shatter,” said Kit. “And I’m thinking, ‘it’s going to be difficult no matter what’.”

Randy said the writing had long been on the wall. They were, after all, on a ship that “drinks petrol by the metric tonne”. “You know, literally they’re buying 150 metric tonnes of fuel at a time,” he said. “We’re talking about $800,000 if we tried to get a full tank.”

While docked in Singapore in August, passengers had already been told the company did not have enough money to continue cruising, and several of the residents had contributed their own funds to get it moving again.

“Very few expect to get any money back because we know that they [the company] have been in terrible money problems from the beginning,” said Randy. Passengers had also passed a jar around for money for the crew, who are also stuck in Cambodia, he said.

Will the story of the Odyssey put people off cruises? It is unlikely, said Prof Andrew Coggins, an industry analyst, who pointed to an unprecedented boom since the end of the Covid pandemic, with global passengers reaching a historical high of 37.2 million in 2025.

Those numbers were in part because of “pent up demand” from those who had been unable to enjoy a cruise during the pandemic years, he said. But it was also the case, he said, that a cruise could offer good value for money. “You get to be pampered, you pack and unpack once, but you see different places, you eat better food than you would get at home, and then you have the romance of going to sea,” he said.

blocks.caption: Going nowhere: the Villa Vie Odyssey at Sihanoukville port in Cambodia. Photograph: Kith Serey/EPA

blocks.text: Residential ships such as the Odyssey were, though, in a very small category of their own, Coggins added. “The World is the only other one I know about and I think there are a couple that are trying to start up,” he said. But the finances are notoriously difficult. In 2023, a three-year cruise offered by Miray Cruises, with fares starting at $30,000 per person per year, including accommodation, food, drinks, laundry and even health care, was cancelled weeks before its due departure date owing to an inability to make the sums add up..

To survive choppy world markets, charges to the passengers have to be high, necessitating a concomitant level of luxury. “The World was actually built as a residential ship,” Coggins said. “The cabins or the state rooms are much bigger.”

Speaking earlier in the week, Mikael Petterson, who launched Villa Vie Residences in 2023, accepted that he was the “villain in the story” but said he was doing everything he could to help the stranded passengers. “Nobody that’s tried residential cruising has succeeded and we have gone further than anyone else,” he said. “But I think we would have been absolutely fine and we would have seen this through, if there was no Iran war.”

Back in Cambodia, Randy has been blogging to keep people updated while they work out what to do next. But he isn’t bitter. For all the promises, he said, all good things must come to an end. “Our message is that we’re not saying ‘poor me’. We know that people are having trouble, that they’re trying to put fuel in their cars, food in their mouths. And we’re very lucky. We’re not crying in our soup. So we are completely aware that we’re very lucky and that we’re going to land on our feet and be OK.”

Kit, a transformation coach, agreed. “This isn’t a pity party for us,” she said. “We actually want to say to people: ‘Live your dreams. Go for the gusto. Live life while you can because you don’t know how the adventure will turn out’.”

articles.title: This record shop owner strives to keep cassette, vinyl music alive
articles.summary: On a regular day, Ge Timbreza of Spin The Reel Music Trade lets his turntable play music for hours on end as he serves customers looking for their own CD, cassette, or vinyl to take home

blocks.text: Ge Timbreza has lived and breathed music for as long as he can remember.
In his younger years, he played in a band with his friends. Then, he started collecting CDs and cassette tapes just for the fun of it.

TImbreza was just in high school when he bought his own cassette player. To this day, the nostalgia of listening to old records hits just as hard — and it’s a feeling he believes he can never replicate from streaming music online.
Timbreza’s love for music didn’t just take him down memory lane. In 2017, it also led him to establish Spin The Reel Music Trade, which now operates daily in Pasig City.
His wife, Charm, has always been supportive of him. His 16-year-old son is also one of the reasons why the business keeps running, since he also inspires him to pursue music.
In the dusty shelves of Spin The Reel Music Trade are decades of history representing the hard work of artists, ready to be reached for by collectors.

For collectors like Timbreza, there is a certain type of magic in being able to feel physical records and play them through turntables, cassette players, and CD players. The process is more personal, where the listener builds their own taste brick by brick, rather than having online algorithms decide the next song they should tune into.

At Spin The Reel Music Trade, unassuming customers turn into regulars, and eventually pass that hobby on to their peers. Clearly, word-of-mouth is a big weapon in the world of analog music. So long as it’s kept alive by collectors and collectors-in-the-making, Timbreza believes the industry will remain.
You’d think that Baby Boomers, Gen X-ers, and millennials would make up a large chunk of a record shop’s customer base. Physical media was what they grew up with after all.

But Timbreza would be in for a surprise when he’d find himself doing business with Gen Zs wanting to buy and collect records of their own. Yes, the same generation that spent much of their teenage years listening to their favorite tracks on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple Music. But there will always be something to go back for when it comes to physical media.
View this post on Instagram A post shared by Spin The Reel Music Trade (@spinthereelmusictrade)

“Marami mga kabataan na gusto ring maranasan ‘yung mga dating physical media. May vinyl, ‘yan. CDs, lalo na CDs, ang dami! Pero siyempre ‘yung mga dating generation na, ‘yung mga medyo ’80s, ’70s na, naghahanap pa rin sila kung ano ‘yung mga gusto nila.”

(There are a lot of young people who also want to experience physical media. Vinyls, CDs, especially CDs, there are a lot! But of course there are older generations from the ’80s and ’70s that still look for records they want.)

Spin The Reel Music Trade stocks a wide range of physical records across different genres and eras. There are “oldies but goodies” that Timbreza himself listens heavily to, like The Beatles, along with modern artists like Taylor Swift.
Of course, the shop is also a gold mine for physical copies of OPM hits — think Eraserheads’ Cutterpillow and Circus, Up Dharma Down’s U D D, and the more recent Grandma by Unique Salonga.
Timbreza, however, is always pleasantly surprised to see the young ones come into his shop looking for older records that they first learned of through their parents.

In online platforms, the algorithm automatically detects your music taste and suggests similar genres you might like. Timbreza, being in the physical records industry, values human interaction and conversations by personally recommending similar genres and music to people who ask.

For Timbreza, manual playlists are better since the listener gets to handpick the music they want to listen to. Later, they get to develop a music taste through human connection rather than fed by the algorithm. These kinds of recommendations are what makes music listening more human.

Connection among business owners like Timbreza and physical records enthusiasts enables personal ears for music. It inspires more people to be musicians, to develop skills in determining what they want to listen to, and eventually, how they want their own music to sound similarly to.

“Iba rin ‘yung generation ngayon ng mga artists. Sila [fellow business owners] din gano’n din, nagtatanong din sa amin, ‘Oh sir, paano ‘yung mga ganito? Ano ba ‘yung mga tugtugan nito?’ Tulungan lang din kami talaga.”
(The generation of artists today are different. Fellow sellers also ask us, ‘Sir, are you familiar with this? What genre of music is this?’ We all help each other.)

If music is a form of expression, physical records give way for more emotions. For Timbreza, turntables produce fuller sounds compared to phones, not just in a literal sense, but in a way that it feels like you’re listening to a song while it’s being recorded live.

“Kumpleto kasi ‘yung instrumento na naririnig mo doon sa tugtog mismo. And sa mga [online streaming platforms] kasi ngayon, lalo na sa Spotify, hindi mo marinig eh. Hindi mo ma-feel eh. Dito kasi sa plaka minsan parang naririnig mo parang nandoon ka sa mismong recording studio nila dati.”
(Instruments you hear in physical records are clearer. Compared to Spotify, you can’t hear some details. You can’t feel much. In physical records, you can feel as if you’re in the recording studio.)
Timbreza also said there were more physical records sellers like him during the early 2000s, but most of them left the industry because of the competition with online platforms.

Online platforms weren’t treated as hindrances for Timbreza’s business. In fact, he utilized social media to do live-selling of his products, especially during the pandemic from 2019 to 2020. Because of that exposure, people online realized that physical records are still being sold, even virtually.
“Mas maganda rin na malaman nila na, “Uy, buhay pa pala… buhay pa pala mga physical media! Mayroon pa rin palang nagbebenta.’”
(It’s still good to let people know that, ‘Oh, it’s still alive… Physical media is still alive! There are still sellers.’)

Pressing plants in the Philippines that used to mass produce vinyls and CDs have stopped operations around early 2004. However, local pressing services still exist, most of which are independent businesses.

“Although sabi naman nila, ‘yung mga talagang collector ng plaka, hindi naman talaga nawala. So nandoon pa rin sa kanila. So ang nawala lang talaga ‘yung mga nagbebenta, pati ‘yung mga stores dati na nagbebenta, nawala din sila eh.”
(Although they said, the collectors of records, they’re never really gone. The records are still with them. What disappeared are the sellers, the stores, they also left.)
He hopes that the Philippines can once again have traditional pressing plants like before. He also advocates to reduce piracy when it comes to buying physical records.

blocks.caption: Record fairs and borrowed nostalgia

blocks.text: “Sana tuloy-tuloy pa rin ‘yung adbokasiya namin hangga’t mayroong physical media na nakukuha sa ibang bansa, o kung may magkaroon man tayo ulit dito ng pressing plant, much better, mas mura.”

(Hopefully our advocacy will continue as long as there is physical media that can be obtained in other countries, or there can be a pressing plant here [in the Philippines] again, much better, much affordable.)
Classics are also designed manually. Even with the rise of AI-generated designs, Timbreza appreciates human-made album covers better.

“Mag-uusbong pa rin in the future ang mga physical media natin. Iba pa rin ‘yung original kasi eh. Iba pa rin. Parang sa mga art din nakita ko, minsan nakikita ko sa ginagawa sa AI ‘yung pag-design-design nila. So I think hindi ‘yan mawawala. Tatagal pa ‘yan, tatagal pa.”

(Physical media will still emerge in the future. Originals still hit differently. Like the art I see today, some designs are AI-generated. So I think it [physical records] won’t be gone. It will last long.)

Timbreza still encourages artists today to release their music through physical records to capture more audiences and inspire their fans to buy more of them. Artists are the forefront of physical media, and they can help in keeping dust away from vinyls.

blocks.caption: Sugarfree’s ‘Dramachine’ gets the classic vinyl treatment

blocks.text: “Para sa akin siguro mas okay pa rin i-release nila nang physical records. Para sa akin talaga mas okay para bumalik pa rin ‘yung mga tao, tsaka mas mabebenta siguro lalo na sa mga fans nila.”
(For me, maybe it’s still better for them to release music as physical records. For me, it’s better so people can also go back, and for them to sell more to their fans.)

Among the music enthusiasts that contribute in keeping physical records such as vinyls, cassette tapes, and CDs alive, Timbreza vows to retain the industry in his bloodline and for more generations to come.

“Sa akin naman kasi tuloy-tuloy lang kami. Tuloy-tuloy lang kami sa pagbenta hanggang sa tumanda na kami. Tuloy-tuloy lang hangga’t kaya, hangga’t buhay pa ang physical media, ipo-promote namin sa mga kabataan pa rin. Kasi feeling ko hindi naman mawawala ‘to eh.”

(For me, we’ll just keep going. We’ll continue to sell until we grow old. Keep going as long as we can, as long as physical media is alive, we promote them to the youth. The feeling will never fade or disappear.) – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump's tariffs could shutter this Canadian town - its residents are fighting to save it
articles.summary: A century-old paper mill in Témiscaming, Quebec is indefinitely closed after the US imposed 50% tariffs on its products, putting hundreds out of work.

blocks.text: "We're going to fight" - How a paper mill's uncertain future could devastate tiny Quebec town
ByJessica MurphyCanada digital editor and Nadine YousifSenior Canada reporter
As you cross the Ottawa river into Témiscaming, Quebec, the paper mill takes up much of the horizon.

The town itself was built over a century ago, around the mill and the region's forests filled with pine, birch, spruce and fir. Now, the main employer and economic anchor sits idle after trade talks broke down between Canada and the US and President Donald Trump imposed more tariffs on the country.
Most of the mill‘s 360 employees are out of work, kept afloat for the moment with partial pay from government tariff-relief.
For some, like Nadine Suley, the shuttering of the mill could mark not just a lost livelihood, but a lost way of life.

She is not "a city girl", and is heading out moose hunting later to take advantage of the short season, like much of the town. She quips they'll all need the free meat provided by the animals this year.
"It's not just a job. It's our home," Suley says, adding that the US tariffs on her town feel like "a personal attack".
In early October, American owner RYAM went ahead with an "economic shutdown" of the mill for "an indefinite period".
Property values in Témiscaming fell almost overnight, and "For Sale" signs dot the yards of modest middle-class homes that make up most of the town.
There are fears that essential service people - from grocery store clerks to the doctors at the small local hospital - could also be on their way out.
"If the mill goes down, it'll turn into a ghost town," says Ronnie Raymond, who like many in the town comes from a family of mill workers.
"There'll be nothing, nothing left. There's no work for anybody, really. It's scary."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The paper mill has served as the economic engine of Témiscaming for over a century.

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Jessica Murphy
The paper mill has served as the economic engine of Témiscaming for over a century.

At a high level, Canada's economy has weathered the ongoing trade war with the US, its largest customer. The national unemployment rate has remained largely steady at around 6.5% since Trump's tariffs were first implemented. It's been coupled with tepid but consistent economic growth.

But a closer look at the numbers shows pockets of deep pain in industries directly hit by US tariffs of up to 50%, like steel, aluminium, automobiles and - in the case of Témiscaming - lumber, pulp and paper. It raises questions about whether the Carney government is doing enough to help those struggling while a trade deal remains elusive.

"If there was 10% of job loss in Toronto or Montreal or Quebec City or Vancouver, it'd be all over the news, and it'd be a lot of pressure on the governments to do something,” says Stéphane Lefebvre, an employee and union leader, whose father and grandfather also worked at the mill.

That economic pain could have ripple effects on the entire forestry industry in the region, including saw mills and trucking. One local contractor told the BBC he has already had to lay off 13 people.

The last time the town faced a threat this existential was in 1973, when the mill's then-American owner threatened to shut it down, prompting the local workers and managers to come together and purchase it.
They turned it into Tembec, a Quebec-owned, international company with branches across North America and France.
The workers now hope to do it again, mobilising a coalition of locals who want to buy the plant back from RYAM, which purchased it in 2017.
"We're hoping that lightning will hit twice," Lefebvre says, speaking inside the town's union hall.
But he contends that they cannot do so without significant help from Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Quebec government, either in the form of tariff relief or financial support.

Suley notes that the prime minister has placed emphasis on "buy local" and supporting Canadian workers since he was elected. Backing the town's bid to buy back the mill, she says, would be a way for Carney to fulfil that pledge.
In an email to the BBC, RYAM said it would not comment on a potential sale of the plant or any prospective buyers.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Stéphane Lefebvre, his father and grandfather all worked at the paper mill in Témiscaming.

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Nadine Yousif
Stéphane Lefebvre, his father and grandfather all worked at the paper mill in Témiscaming.
Mayor Alain Gauthier doesn't blame RYAM for its decision. He calls US tariffs "a bomb to shut down our manufacturing in Canada".
He wants Ottawa to retaliate with its own duties on the board products coming into Canada from the US, currently tariff-free.
And he says that while politicians have said Canada is in an economic war with the US, "in reality we see absolutely no evidence of war measures being taken".
"We feel we got into a war with kid's water guns to fight back."
Some, like Lefebvre, feel that forestry has taken a back seat in the fight to save other tariffed industries like steel and autos.

This month, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly threatened Stelco - one of Canada's largest steelmakers - with financial penalties or a forced asset sale should they go ahead with the planned layoffs of some 500 workers due to steel tariffs pressure.
Stelco in Hamilton, near Toronto, is owned by US-based Cleveland-Cliffs, which committed to keeping jobs in Canada when it bought the firm in 2024.

Last week, Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced nearly C$9bn ($6.4bn; £4.8bn) to help Ontario's steel and auto sector. The funds will be used to help the industries modernise, strengthen domestic demand and open new markets overseas, they said.

Sébastien Lemire, the elected MP for Témiscaming from the Bloc Québécois party, told the BBC that he is "very concerned and worried" about what he calls inaction from the Carney government to support the town and Quebec's forestry industry more broadly.
A spokesperson for Minister Joly told the BBC in a statement that the government has made available $400m to support the forestry sector in rural and remote areas.
It has also launched a programme to help businesses impacted by tariffs to access cash-flow while they work to pivot away from US markets.

On the Témiscaming mill, the spokesperson said that the government "is actively working with all parties involved to find a viable solution to the issues facing the company, while responsibly managing Canadians' dollars."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Témiscaming residents gathered for a Union-led rally to support the mill's workers and draw attention to the woes of the lumber industry.

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied/Stéphane Lefebvre
Témiscaming residents gathered for a Union-led rally to support the mill's workers and draw attention to the woes of the lumber industry.
In August, after the breakdown in trade talks, the US imposed 50% duties on a some C$28bn of Canadian goods, including wood and paper products like pulp, stationery and boxes.
Canada in response imposed its own "dollar-for-dollar" counter-tariffs.

The Témiscaming mill, which produces paperboard used in frozen-food packaging across North America and in the scratch-off lottery tickets commonly found at convenience stores, sends roughly 75% of its production to the US.
Trump argues these import taxes boost US manufacturing and create jobs - essentially seeking to protect US workers who could face similar fates to those in Témiscaming.
Frank Dottori has been through all of this before.

Now in his 80s and retired in Témiscaming, he was an engineer at the mill that was instrumental in organising its employees in the 1970s to take a 10% cut in order to collectively purchase it. He went on to become CEO.
Their ambitions were seen as foolish at the time, and he recalls being "politely ejected" by the Quebec premier when he first came knocking for support.
But they prevailed with the help of the labour union and an ex-employee with executive experience and plenty of swagger. Dottori attributes their success to this person's forceful charisma.
Dottori said the new generation of workers need someone just as bold.
"Does the local group have that? Highly unlikely. Can they get it? Yeah, if they if they organise themselves," he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Frank Dottori led the effort to buy the Témiscaming mill in the 1970s during a period of economic hardship

blocks.text: Frank Dottori led the effort to buy the Témiscaming mill in the 1970s during a period of economic hardship
It is also imperative, he says, that US tariffs be lifted to restore the mill's long-term economic viability, at least in the short term.

Many workers in Témiscaming say they are placing some hope in the upcoming US midterm elections to put pressure on Trump — whose approval ratings have fallen among Americans, according to polls — to ease some of his tariffs on Canada.
"We'll take any help we can get," Suley says, adding: "There are Americans that care what's going on, and it's affecting them too."

There are signs the Trump administration is taking note of that pressure, with some tariffs on Canadian goods lifted last week after lobbying from Republican Maine Senator Susan Collins, who is running for re-election in November. Those changes don't apply to products made at Témiscaming's mill, however.
Suley and others hope a resolution will come quickly, before winter, when sub-zero temperatures could freeze equipment at the idle plant, causing damage that would make reopening even more difficult.
In the meantime, Lefebvre says he is committed to making the dream of local ownership of the mill a reality, regardless of what happens.
"We're in Game Seven right now," he says. "We're gonna play till the last whistle."

articles.title: Crypto exchanges call for quick moves to bolster defenses after Binance heist
articles.summary: Rival crypto exchanges move quickly to shore up their own systems and to reassure customers their tokens were safe

blocks.text: CRYPTO. Representation of cryptocurrencies are seen in this illustration taken September 10, 2025.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
Rival crypto exchanges move quickly to shore up their own systems and to reassure customers their tokens were safe

items: Crypto exchanges are enhancing their security measures and advocating for industry-wide information sharing following a significant $6.3-billion hack of Binance, which exposed vulnerabilities in the sector.

Binance halted withdrawals after the attack, believed to be linked to North Korea, and plans to cover the losses with company funds, while other exchanges like Coinbase and Kraken are adjusting their systems and monitoring for potential threats.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Crypto exchanges are taking quick action to bolster their defenses and urging greater industry-wide information-sharing after a record $6.3 billion hack of Binance exposed their vulnerability just as they become more embedded in mainstream finance.

Coinbase said it made adjustments to its systems that store cryptocurrency keys offline “solely out of an abundance of caution,” while Kraken said it was monitoring industry incidents for lessons it could apply to its defenses.

But the industry will need to move urgently, analysts and industry executives said, as President Donald Trump’s regulators promote deeper integration of digital assets into the financial system, raising the stakes for an industry with a history of big hacks.

blocks.caption: Crypto exchange Binance freezes assets after $6.3-billion security breach

blocks.text: “For crypto to reach its full potential, the security situation must be addressed immediately,” said Chris Perkins, Franklin Templeton’s head of crypto.
Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, halted withdrawals after Thursday’s attack — which analysts blamed on North Korea — and said it would use company funds to cover the losses.

Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on X that the “complex attack” may have begun with a compromised software engineer’s laptop, giving hackers access to systems used to process withdrawals. The company later found additional breaches, while software designed to erase traces of the attack hampered the investigation.
Rival crypto exchanges moved quickly on Friday, October 30, to shore up their own systems and to reassure customers that their tokens were safe
“Full-time teams at Kraken look for potential vulnerabilities every day,” a Kraken spokesperson said.

Still, even as the industry reeled from the biggest cryptocurrency heist of all time, executives expressed confidence that Binance had sufficient resources to cover the losses and that the hack would not have broader financial repercussions.
Bitcoin fell more than 4% on Thursday while ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency, fell more than 5%, although both tokens recovered some of that ground on Friday.

“Our expectation is the industry writ large will actually not suffer material losses, even though Binance is obviously going to have to deal with the exploit directly,” said Josh Riezman, chief legal and strategy officer at crypto firm GSR.

The bulk of the heist unfolded in around 20 minutes late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous attacks blamed on North Korea, according ​to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
North Korea routinely denies involvement in cryptocurrency thefts, and its mission in Geneva did not respond to requests for comment.

While much remains unclear, social engineering, a common tactic in which hackers trick victims into revealing sensitive information or granting access to systems, may have been involved in compromising the laptop, security experts said.
Harry Donnelly, CEO of Circuit, a crypto risk infrastructure company, said companies are planning more employee training to guard against social engineering attacks.

In such attacks, hackers race to launder the funds before the exchange detects the breach and token issuers freeze assets. Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion linked to Binance, while Circle said it froze $800 million. Bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen because no single entity controls the coins.
Chainalysis said the hackers appeared to be using sophisticated laundering patterns it had not seen before.
On Friday, some crypto exchange executives called for the industry to develop a coordinated hack detection system.

“We need a real-time alert system that allows participants to share information immediately when a hack occurs, coordinate a rapid response, and temporarily freeze suspected stolen funds,” said Star Xu, CEO of crypto exchange OKX, in a post on X.

GSR’s Riezman added that the Binance hack could spur the industry to act: “As we’re at this kind of confluence moment for traditional finance and digital assets, I think it’s obviously important that we continue to improve, and I think this, if anything, will be a catalyst for that.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Albanese looks for reset on world stage as ‘spot fires burn’ domestically and likely interest rate hike looms
articles.summary:
The prime minister will speak with King Charles and others at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda

  • Get our

blocks.text: As “summit season” begins, reaffirming ties with fellow leaders on the world stage could be a circuit breaker for Anthony Albanese amid domestic and economic woes, analysts have said.
But a likely interest rate hike triggered by higher-than-expected inflation while the prime minister is overseas will make his job – and the treasurer’s – even harder.
Albanese is attending the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda from Saturday.
He will hold talks with King Charles III and allies including the UK and Canadian prime ministers, Andy Burnham and Mark Carney, at the biennial meeting.

The discussions will constitute a well-needed reset after controversies over grant funding and pressures on inflation, according to Dr Zareh Ghazarian, an associate professor of politics at Monash University.
“It is a strategically important time for him,” Ghazarian said.
“He’s got a lot of spot fires burning domestically but this is going to be an opportunity for him to present himself to be much more on the front foot.
“There’s a lot of pressure, so this trip could just be a moment to reset the political debate for people … this is a critical moment to present himself as a world leader amongst other world leaders.”
Albanese will be away when the Reserve Bank hands down its next interest rate decision on Tuesday, with markets tipping a rise to 4.85%.
It would be the fifth interest rate hike in 2026 and a challenging situation for the government to navigate, amid continuing cost-of-living pressures.

Albanese emphasised the value of attending Chogm before his departure on Saturday morning. In a crowded international calendar, the Commonwealth is occasionally dismissed as irrelevant, an anachronistic relic of a former imperial era.
“The Commonwealth heads of government meeting is an important forum,” Albanese said.
“[It provides] an opportunity to work with some of our closest partners on shared challenges, including climate change, the preservation of our oceans, trade and investment and the rise of AI.”
after newsletter promotion
The issue of historical slavery, and its ongoing legacy, is likely to be a key point of contention at Chogm.
Burnham, writing in the Guardian, said having “difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future” was the right thing to do.
“Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.”
He called the transatlantic slave trade a “brutal and barbaric violation” of people “treated as property and worked to their deaths”.
“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” he wrote.
Caribbean nations have made renewed calls for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit, and for reparations, as the King toured the Caribbean.

Burnham said: “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them.” But he said he did not believe reparations for slavery was the “right answer”.
Australia would not be a bystander to any debate about slavery and the slave trade.

Across the 19th and early 20th centuries, Australian agriculture relied heavily on “blackbirding”: the use of coercion, trickery, bribery and kidnapping to bring more than 60,000 Pacific Islanders to work as indentured labourers in Australia, primarily on Queensland’s sugar and cotton plantations.
The Chogm meeting will kick off a busy end to the year overseas for Albanese, with international summits in Turkey, the Philippines, China and the US in coming weeks.

The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, is currently in Atlanta, Georgia for the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting. The start of that conference has been overshadowed by the presence of Russia, with about one-third of the countries attending vowing to boycott the customary “family photo” if the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, was involved.

articles.title: ‘You have my word, sir’: Macacua’s hat tip to Murad
articles.summary: ‘This is my commitment to you, and an amanah I intend to honor,’ Bangsamoro chief minister Abdulraof Macacua tells Ahod Ebrahim in front of members of parliament on October 30

blocks.text: GESTURE. BARMM chief minister Abdulraof Macacua leans to kiss the temple of MILF chairman Ahod "Al Haj Murad" Ebrahim during the inaugural session of the regular parliament on Friday, October 30.
Photo from Abdulraof Macacua
‘This is my commitment to you, and an amanah I intend to honor,’ Bangsamoro chief minister Abdulraof Macacua tells Ahod Ebrahim in front of members of parliament on October 30

items: Abdulraof Macacua was elected as the new Bangsamoro chief minister, defeating his predecessor Ahod 'Al Haj Murad' Ebrahim with 51 votes to 27.
Despite a rocky history and tensions within the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), Macacua expressed respect for Murad and committed to continuing the moral governance agenda established by him.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Abdulraof Macacua, the newly-installed Bangsamoro chief minister, started his term with a deference and a nod to his predecessor, Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim.
The election of the first chief minister in the region’s regular parliament was a battle between Macacua and Murad. The result was as predicted. Macacua garnered 51 votes while Murad got 27 votes.
Near the end of his inaugural address on Friday, October 30, Macacua addressed Murad in front of the 80-member parliament:

“To our chairman in the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, the Honorable Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim. Sir, I want to personally assure you that the moral governance agenda you have started and steadfastly championed will remain at the very heart of my leadership.”

Macacua and Murad’s recent history had been rocky since President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. installed Macacua as interim chief minister to replace Murad in 2025. What followed was a widening of rifts within the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF).
In the run up to the elections, Macacua ran as an independent and later on became chairman of the newfound Bangsamoro Federalist Party. Macacua’s rivaled the MILF’s United Bangsamoro Justice Party.

And months before the elections, Macacua was suspended as MILF’s military chief for being “inconsistent” with the group’s political line. His moves had upset members and supporters of the MILF, those who remain loyal to Murad’s leadership.
Despite the divergence, Macacua was said to still retain a certain respect to Murad. Macacua, after all, was Murad’s subordinate in the MILF.

But all that is in the past now. It seemed the two have reached an impasse after the violent election and the huge gap between votes. As Macacua leads the new government, the MILF leadership will be at work seeing the peace process with the Philippine government come to its conclusion.

Macacua returned to the work that became the foundation of the regular parliament the region now has today: “I recognize the sacrifices, principles, and aspirations upon which this vision was built, and I consider it both a personal commitment and a moral responsibility to carry it forward, no matter what. You have my word, Sir, that I will remain faithful to this vision, not only in words but in every decision and action of this administration, until the very last day of my mandate.”
He ended his message to Murad with a promise. “This is my commitment to you, and an amanah I intend to honor.”

blocks.caption: ‘You have my word, sir’: Macacua’s hat tip to Murad

blocks.text: The inaugural session was a portent of things to come.
Macacua’s message of inclusion followed a heated exchange in the plenary hall.
This started when the majority moved to elect their full list of officers to committee heads.

items: Deputy chief ministers: Hadjimar Matba for the southwestern Mindanao subregion and Mamintal Adiong III for the north central Mindanao subregion
Deputy speakers: Rhosatina Matolo-De Asis, Tawakal Buga Midtimbang, Amilbahar Mawalil, Ibrahim Ibay, Hosni Macapodi, Lampa Pandi, Ahmad Amir Balindong, Suwaib Oranon, Abrar Hataman, and Jose Lorena.
Majority floor leader: Johari Abu
Deputy majority floor leaders: Abdel Razi Amin, Naguib Sinarimbo, Ishak Mastura, Jaafar Matalam, Alindatu Pagayao, Jay Hatman Salliman, Julbert Que, and Tomanda Antok

blocks.caption: SESSION. Inaugural session of the Bangsamoro Parliament on Friday, October 30. Screenshot from RTVM

blocks.text: Member of parliament Mary Ann Arnado, who won as the settler community representative under the United Bangsamoro Justice Party, raised concerns in behalf of the minority.

“We would also like to organize the minority by nominating our minority floor leader and our deputies – the deputies of the floor leader,” said member of parliament Mary Ann Arnado. “I hope that the majority will not disagree with that.”
Member of parliament Naguib Sinarimbo defended the majority, who he said was formed by parties and members of parliament who agreed to constitute the government of the day.
“If the government of the day has been constituted, then those who did not join the coalition of the majority cannot insist on representing themselves in the government of the day,” said Sinrimbo.
The first session ended without a minority floor leader being elected, as Arnado and her allies proposed.

Prior to this, the Bangsamoro Federalist Party has claimed support of 46 out of the 80 members in parliament and subsequently forming the majority. Forming a coalition to make a majority had been the primary work of the parties after the September 14 election resulted to a hung parliament. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy praises US over $2.1bn Patriot missile deal but warns it could take years
articles.summary:
The Ukrainian president called the US decision strong, but added that delivery of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles ⁠could take years

The US has approved the sale ⁠of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles ⁠to…

blocks.text: The US has approved the sale ⁠of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles ⁠to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1bn, but Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned deliveries could take years and stockpiles were needed now to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.

“The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capabilities,” the US state department said in a statement on Friday.
The statement did not provide an estimate for when the weapons could be delivered to Ukraine.

Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision by the US state department” but said in a post on X early on Saturday: “However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS. We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors.
“Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day.”

Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves ⁠of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.

On Thursday, a Russian drone ​strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform ‌in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while five ‌died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed 1 person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.

Zelenskyy said US and European allies had sufficient stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to provide to Ukraine now, which could be replenished in the coming years through contracts already paid for by Ukraine and its partners.
He said this would “be the right approach” and was “entirely feasible”.

Delayed missile deliveries have added to Kyiv’s tensions with Washington ⁠after US president Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Zelenskyy for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.

But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will probably not receive the missile interceptors quickly. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles – which are yet to be manufactured – are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.

One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense was encouraging the Pentagon to bring ‌forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.

Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US Jumpstart, ​along with national funds financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan, the state department said in a statement.
The programme uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defence following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.

The US has ⁠supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, ​raising concerns about inventories of key air defense ​and precision-guided weapons.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
articles.summary: If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
ByLily Jamali
North America Technology correspondent

Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprits in the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.
The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis.
This incident is just the latest linked to the country, one of the poorest in the world and where access to the internet is severely restricted.
Experts accuse the government of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of relying on cybercrime to finance itself, something Pyongyang has long denied.

Though not financial, the nation's most spectacular suspected hack took place in 2014. The target: Sony Pictures, which had made the Hollywood film The Interview. The film involves a plot to assassinate Kim.
The resulting hack exposed thousands of embarrassing emails exchanged among the studio's top executives.
Last year, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange.

In the aftermath of that incident, the agency said TraderTraitor had moved to quickly launder and disperse the stolen assets, converting them to Bitcoin and other digital assets with a goal of eventually turning them into hard currency.
The FBI has broadly accused North Korea of "illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities".

The nation has systematically developed its cyber operations, recruiting the most promising students from universities and channeling them into hacker groups overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, according to reports.
Some of the cyberwarfare conducted takes place just over the nation's border in China, according to analysis from tech groups.
Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affected
Much of its hacking activity has centred on monetary gain.
North Korean hackers are also suspected in the theft of $620m worth of cryptocurrency in 2022.

In this most recent heist, North Korean agents are accused of using a special authorisation to turn a Binance hot wallet, which is connected to the internet, into one that moved funds automatically to the attacker.
TRM said it's likely the attacker gained access to Binance's hot wallet signing system as part of the scheme.
Binance has not directly responded to the BBC's queries about the incident's potential links to the area.
The company had initially said it thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.
"Our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said.
Some 80% of stolen assets have been secured, a Binance spokesperson said on Friday, but the rest remains unaccounted for.
If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become – a sign that the tools of the hacking trade have grown sharper.
Experts say the rise of artificial intelligence has also given threat actors new ways to carry out crime, through automation and other means.
In this case, it's plausible that AI was used to infiltrate Binance's systems.
As Chainalysis put it, the attacker used laundering patterns "we have not seen before".

articles.title: The Indian chef who brought curry to America - then vanished
articles.summary: Indian chef Ranji Smile opened America’s first Indian restaurant in 1901 - then became a fake prince.

blocks.text: The Indian chef who brought curry to America - then vanished

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ranji Smile was one of the most colourful and enigmatic figures to shape the American food scene

blocks.text: Image source, Courtesy: Dinyar Patel
Ranji Smile was one of the most colourful and enigmatic figures to shape the American food scene
One hundred and twenty-five years ago, in 1901, an Indian chef opened what was almost certainly the first Indian restaurant in the US.
Ranji Smile was one of the most colourful and enigmatic figures to shape the American food scene.
In the summer of 1899, Smile sailed from London to New York. We know hardly anything about his origins and early life, not even his real name.
"Ranji" was probably a nod to the Indian cricketing sensation KS Ranjitsinhji, then a star attraction at Test matches in Britain. "Smile" could have been an anglicisation of "Ismail".

Whatever his origins, Smile possessed an uncommon knack for reinvention. Once through the portals of Ellis Island, he appended a new name to his identity, something more in keeping with America's egalitarian promise: Joe.
Joe Ranji Smile arrived in New York to work at Sherry's Restaurant, a glittering new establishment on Fifth Avenue.

In London, he had been a curry cook at the Cecil and Savoy hotels. Here, according to an 1899 profile in Harper's, he was noticed by Sherry's owner, Louis Sherry, who invited him to bring his culinary skills across the Atlantic. Late Victorian London already boasted an Indian dining scene: as early as 1810, Sake Dean Mohamed, a native of Patna, had opened his Hindostanee Coffee House near Portman Square, plying customers with both curry and hookah.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A party at New York's Sherry restaurant in 1900

blocks.text: Image source, Hulton Archive/Getty Images
A party at New York's Sherry restaurant in 1900

Manhattanite tastebuds lacked much exposure to masala. There was, however, growing curiosity about India and its culture. Swami Vivekananda, the spellbinding orator and exponent of Hindu philosophy, enthralled audiences during his visits to the city in the 1890s. At the same time, more Indian sailors, students and professionals trickled into New York. This was probably why Louis Sherry decided to add a curry cook to his kitchen staff.

At Sherry's Restaurant, Smile joined one of the great culinary institutions of the American Gilded Age. Positioning itself as a rival to Delmonico's, New York's byword for fine dining, Sherry's catered to city plutocrats like the Astors and was famed for over-the-top dining experiences. During one such soiree, patrons marched their horses into a ballroom, saddled up and ate on horseback.
Smile, a skilled showman, thrived in this environment.
Customers soon flocked to taste his preparations of Bombay duck, a glutinous lizardfish that is a delicacy along the western Indian coast, and novel creations like "Lettuce Ceylon".

Cooking and serving became a performance. Dressed in a satin coat and blue silk turban, Smile salaamed in front of customers before enquiring, "Will you have the curry hot or mild, sahib?" Pictures of Sherry's curry chef were soon splashed across newspapers and magazines. One headline said it all: "New York women go wild over him."

As his fame grew, Smile decided in 1901 to leave Sherry's and set up his own establishment, one exclusively devoted to Indian cuisine. For financial backing, he leaned on Roland R Conklin, a prominent financier, external and the inventor of an early version of the motorhome.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A Washington Post headline on Ranji Smile in 1907

blocks.text: A Washington Post headline on Ranji Smile in 1907

Omar Khayyam, Smile's Indian restaurant, opened in late 1901 at 325 Fifth Avenue. This was prime real estate, a block away from the original Waldorf-Astoria Hotel where, 29 years later, the Empire State Building would rise. Smile adorned the restaurant with Indian draperies and hanging lanterns.

As the New York Herald reported, a fleet of Indian waiters in "voluminous turbans" staffed the premises, as did a group of Indian musicians. Now quite the embodiment of the American immigrant success story, Smile eagerly awaited his customers and fans.
Alas, they never materialised. Within a year, Omar Khayyam shuttered. The New York Sun claimed that people had "tired" of Indian fare, dismissing it as a passing fad.
Smile's stardom, which had blazed so brightly in the Big Apple, also began to dim. Unfortunately, his showmanship and flare for theatrics shaded into deceit and criminal activity.

Smile began claiming that he was, after all, not an everyday Joe but rather a prince, the son of the emir of Baluchistan, a fictional title. And, before opening Omar Khayyam, he made a quick visit to Bombay, where he pronounced himself to be a guest at the upcoming coronation of King Edward VII in London and recruited a retinue of staff: valets, a dancing girl, and "mahouts to drive his herds of elephants".

All of this was reported in New York newspapers like the Times because, as a subsequent federal case against him alleged, Smile illegally trafficked this staff into the US to work at his restaurant. Instead of becoming a pioneer outpost of Indian gastronomy, Omar Khayyam nearly got Smile deported.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Violet Ethel Rochlitz, Smile's wife, was featured in the Salt Lake City Tribune in 1913

blocks.text: Violet Ethel Rochlitz, Smile's wife, was featured in the Salt Lake City Tribune in 1913

"Prince" Joe Ranji Smile evaded deportation (many in his retinue were not as lucky) and went on evolving his invented persona, all while wooing and marrying a series of impressionable young American women. He began claiming that Indian food was a secret elixir for female beauty. "The eye will grow lustrous, the complexion will be yet so lovely," Smile promised, displaying his wives as clinching proof.
Meanwhile, he honed his performing skills at Indian cooking demonstrations across the country.

In Washington DC, Smile prepared dishes, including a dubious-sounding dessert called "bungalow", while a juggler and dancing girl entertained him. On his way to Chicago, as one newspaper in remote Idaho reported, he declared himself to be no longer the son of the emir but the brother of an even more fanciful figure, the "great Beglerberg of Baluchistan". If Smile was guilty of being a conman, then his American interlocutors were equally guilty of wide-eyed gullibility.
While Smile's theatrics and good food kept people entertained for a while, the tall tales and outright fabrications soon caught up with him.

Smile retreated from the public gaze, hurt by further brushes with the law which ranged from forcible confinement of one of his dancing girls to refusing to pay a bill at an Italian restaurant in Manhattan. By the 1920s, he apparently abandoned cooking entirely, listing his occupation as a merchant.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The New Haven Union in 1912 ran a story on 'Mr and Mrs Ranji Smile'.

blocks.text: The New Haven Union in 1912 ran a story on 'Mr and Mrs Ranji Smile'.

The final shred of evidence about Smile dates from 1937, when his fourth or fifth American wife approached the New York Supreme Court and filed for an annulment of her marriage to her now-absconded husband. Ranji Smile's last act of reinvention was to simply disappear.
Despite this inglorious end, Smile and his Indian restaurant did pave the way for the popularisation of Indian cuisine in America. Other immigrants soon tested the waters.
In 1909, Saint Nihal Singh, a peripatetic journalist from Punjab, introduced readers of the Chicago Daily Tribune to recipes for bhajias, puris, halwa, and "Fried Chicken a la Hindoo".

Aware of the unfamiliarity of many Indian ingredients amongst Chicagoans, Singh urged readers to look for them in the city's Chinese grocery stores. On another occasion, which might make contemporary chefs blush, he suggested that hamburger meat was an adequate substitute for preparing gosht pilau (a meat pilaf).
Not long after Ranji Smile was hauled to court for trafficking immigrants, a young man from Ceylon named KY Kira arrived at Ellis Island.

blocks.caption: Image caption, KY Kira opened a successful Indian restaurant in New York in 1913

blocks.text: KY Kira opened a successful Indian restaurant in New York in 1913

Like Smile, he had a talent for reinvention. Kira joined a troupe of Sinhalese dancers which performed for American circuses like Barnum and Bailey and Ringling Brothers. In 1913, he opened an Indian restaurant in Harlem, eventually called the Ceylon India Inn. Unlike Omar Khayyam, the Ceylon India Inn was a hit.

New York now had a much larger immigrant Indian population and the restaurant attracted expatriate nationalists and revolutionaries. But it also benefited from a burgeoning American interest in Indian culture and food. By the 1920s, Kira's restaurant, now located off Times Square, catered to Broadway and Hollywood stars. The Ceylon India Inn remained in business until the late 1980s, touting itself as the first Indian restaurant in America.

That, of course, was not the case. Ranji Smile might be long forgotten, but 125 years after the brief existence of his Omar Khayyam restaurant, his legacy lives on in the thousands of Indian eateries flourishing across the US.
Dinyar Patel is associate professor of history at SPJIMR in Mumbai

articles.title: Everywhere, all at once: The year of Nour Hooshmand
articles.summary: A former theater stand-in, Filipino-Iranian actress Nour Hooshmand wants to ‘pave a new path’ for herself, opting for purposeful roles, no matter the screen time

blocks.text: Some years ago, while studying theater arts at the University of the Philippines, Nour Hooshmand would always look forward to the rehearsals of Dulaang UP. There, she was supposed to learn direction and lighting design under the tutelage of the likes of Dexter Santos and the late Floy Quintos, but would instead hone her penchant for performance as a stand-in for actors who couldn’t make it to practice sessions.
She was beside herself for having to act with such accomplished thespians as Shamaine Buencamino and Stella Cañete.

“I enjoyed it so much to the point that I’d wish some actors would not come to the rehearsals so I could do their parts,” said Hooshmand. Her directors would even hand her notes clandestinely, despite knowing she wasn’t there as an understudy.
“Kahit hindi ako ‘yong mag-act sa show pero ‘yong makaeksena ko lang sila even just for a moment, okay na sa akin ‘yon,” Hooshmand continued. “I never really expected na may future dito.”

(Even though I’m not the one acting in the show, just getting to share a scene with them, even if only for a moment, is enough for me. I never really expected that there would be a future for me here.)
At the time, Hooshmand thought she was meant to remain behind the curtains, learning everybody’s blocking and knowing their lines by heart, but never stepping on stage, let alone performing.

“Malala talaga ‘yong battle ko with self-image (My battle with self-image is really bad),” she revealed. She would often hear comments about the implausibility of her becoming an actor and landing roles due to her facial features.
“‘Di raw ako pang-leading lady (They say I’m not leading-lady material),” she said.

Today, the Filipino-Iranian actress is practically everywhere and impossibly hard to miss. Even for the briefest of moments as in David Corpuz’s Tayo Lang Ang Nakakaalam, one of three films at this year’s Cinemalaya that featured her, or in a scene with Judy Ann Santos in the HBO series Call My Manager. A month later, she would win her first acting award at Cinepanalo for her work in the short film Starfish.

She also appeared in Katski Flores’ historical drama Edjop, as well as in three films that all premiered at various film festivals abroad, including Rafael Manuel’s Filipiñana, the Philippines’ official bet for the 2027 Best International Feature Oscar race, John Torres’ The Remotes, and, finally, Arvin Belarmino’s debut feature Ria, Hooshmand’s second lead role, which just played at the Busan International Film Festival.
Porvenir’s El Fuego del Alma, an adaptation of Tennessee Williams’ Summer and Smoke, likewise saw her return to theater.
Not bad for someone still in her late 20s. For someone who supposedly didn’t look the part. For someone people didn’t think could do it — including, for a long time, herself.

Sometime in 2024, after a suggestion from three people, the actress auditioned for the titular role of Ria, though she was initially asked to test for Kim, Iana Bernardez’s part in the film. That day, she was terribly under the weather, too tapped out to even buy food, and was dealing with heartbreaking news about their home. But she proceeded with the audition anyway.
Theater artist Mijon Cortez, who was among the hundreds of applicants, sensed Hooshmand was about to pass out and decided to get her something to eat, while waiting for her turn.

“I feel like kung hindi niya ako binilhan ng pagkain, hindi ako nakapag-perform the way I did,” said Hooshmand, recalling how crucial the gesture was, given the audition had no script and required her to improvise based on a scenario.
(I feel like if he hadn’t bought me food, I wouldn’t have been able to perform the way I did.)

“Ang galing kasi parang the universe gave me a cosmic baggage so that I could relate in a way na hindi ko kailangang umarte nang sobra,” she said. “Dine-describe pa lang ni direk ‘yong eksena, tumutulo na ‘yong luha ko.”

(It’s actually amazing, it’s as if the universe handed me some cosmic baggage, allowing me to relate to things in a way that doesn’t require me to overact. The director was just describing the scene, but my tears were already falling.)
Hooshmand got the part and decided to focus on the project, dropping another title role offered by another international production.

Belarmino and Kyla Romero’s Agapito, which premiered at last year’s Cannes Film Festival and is now campaigning for Best Live Action Short Film at the 99th Academy Awards, was in part shot to test the waters for Ria, since Hooshmand had not met both filmmakers prior to her audition.

blocks.caption: Nour Hooshmand in the short film ‘Agapito.’ Photo courtesy of Cannes website

blocks.text: Ria finds the actress playing a young woman protecting her folk-punk community against the threat of demolition, in a film that is less interested in crystallizing any sense of inner life than it is in weaponizing its languidness.

Positioned to bear the film’s entire political messaging, Hooshmand is arresting in her rage, in her resolve to fight for her found family and the less fortunate, which eventually whisks us off to a closing frame in which she meets the camera’s gaze and shatters it altogether, a final gesture that’s surprisingly less bleak than the rest of the proceedings.

Throwing herself into preparation involved forming a folk-punk band called Karnal with the cast and crew and playing in the local community, on top of organizing film screenings and “food, not bombs” feeding programs.
With all those immersions, Hooshmand was well aware of the sheer magnitude of what she had to take on.

“I know that while I understand what they’re fighting for, I wouldn’t be able to grasp their lived experiences as deeply as they could,” she explained. “There were many occasions where I would pray to the spirits of the punks who had passed away to help me bridge their stories with truth.”

It came to a point that the rage lodged inside Ria began to take a heavy toll on the actress playing her, heightened by the tragic demise of Hooshmand’s Iranian father while shooting the film. She even dreamed of her father on the day they wrapped production.
“I was lucky that Direk Arvin was there,” she said. “He was really my anchor. He never abandoned me, despite all the struggle I went through.”
For Hooshmand, it has always been an accumulation of constantly showing up, putting in the work, gaining confidence, getting people to put their faith in her, and loving the craft.

“It’s always about the process,” she said. “I feel like I’m always a work in progress. I’m always learning from everyone I worked with, whether that be a veteran filmmaker or a student director. That’s what I would want to keep for as long as I work in this industry.”

That eagerness to learn includes completing Ricky Lee’s screenwriting lab earlier this year, or undergoing a Meisner acting workshop alongside friend and Filipiñana co-star Jorybell Agoto three years ago.
Hooshmand credits Agoto, now in critical condition due to her battle with cancer, as among the first people who helped her find her bearings early in her career.

“I really love her as a human being and as an artist,” she said of Agoto, who was celebrating her birthday on the day of the interview. “I just hope that she gets better real soon. Marami pa kaming gagawin (We still have a lot to do).”

She learned of Agoto’s condition earlier this year but opted not to pry into it for her friend’s privacy, and instead, just offered her support and accompanied Agoto during the press tour for Filipiñana.
“I know how exhausting it was to promote a film, and I really wanted to be with her,” she said.

This kind of kinship has always been there since they first worked together in Kevin Mayuga’s When This Is All Over, in the way they share roots in theater, in the way their zodiacs go well together — Agoto is a Libra, Hooshmand is an Aquarius.
“Kaya naming mag-usap hanggang umaga (We can talk until morning).”

Hooshmand’s interest in the arts was first nurtured at home. “Noong bata kasi ako, sobrang hilig ko maglaro. Sobrang hilig ko gumawa ng imagined worlds (When I was a child, I really loved to play. I was very fond of creating imagined worlds). I guess it’s rooted in that playfulness,” she said.

Her mother Belinda was a founding member of Teatro Tomasino, the official theater guild of the University of Santo Tomas, which has remained active since the Martial Law era. Her brother is a devoted musician, while her sister is a massive hoarder of bootleg DVDs, which would introduce her to the allure of the movies.
“I’m lucky that I’m surrounded with this kind of people who pushed me to be creative and pursue the arts,” said Hooshmand.

Such artistic spirit would only heighten growing up and eventually led her to the Diliman campus and to the late National Artist for Theater Tony Mabesa, who, in 2018, would cast Hooshmand in her first lead role on stage, in Dulaang UP’s adaptation of Luigi Pirandello’s Six Characters in Search of an Author, one of the last plays Mabesa would bring to life.

“It was so demanding and difficult. I had to really transform, but it gave me courage,” said Hooshmand. “Na-feel ko kahit papaano na baka kaya ko ngang umarte kasi naniwala siya sa akin, eh (I felt, in a way, that maybe I actually could act because he believed in me).”
Her time in the state university almost entirely revolved around Dulaang UP, given the lore behind its theater-making and Mabesa’s methods.

“We were there every day,” recalled Hooshmand. “When we’re not in class, we’re building sets, we’re building props. It really grounds you in how much time and effort and collaboration it takes to build a production. So that’s my core.”
“Hindi ka puwedeng maging mayabang. Sasaktan ka nila. Naabutan ko ‘yong era na ‘yon. Pinanday nila ‘yong pagkatao ko,” she added.
(You can’t be arrogant. They’ll hurt you. I lived through that era. They shaped my character.)

The pivot to acting in film, however, would not happen immediately. After college, Hooshmand took an office job at the Cultural Center of the Philippines. Then came the pandemic and the bouts of depression that followed when the working environment around her tipped into machinic existence. She longed for her creative side.
Fan Girl, Antoinette Jadaone’s coming-of-age drama, kept her going.
Lounging on a rooftop with her best friend Joshua Chan, she shouted into the cosmos that she would one day work with Jadaone. Of course, she knew it was a long shot.

A week later, she received a call asking her to tape and send an audition for an ad she hardly had any details about. She got a Zoom callback the next day where she met Jadaone, who, to the actor’s surprise, was set to direct the project.
“Hindi ako makapaniwala,” she said. “Ang serendipitous na lang ng mga bagay after that.”
(I can’t believe it. Things just turned out so serendipitously after that.)

That unexpected booking became her way into the industry. And so began the grind, from TV series The Kangks Show, also directed by Jadaone, and Sleep with Me, to the Cinemalaya-winning film Blue Room, and to all her projects that came and will come out this year, including the Netflix series BuyBust: The Undesirables, directed by Erik Matti, which has been in development for years.

But even then, life hasn’t radically transformed for Hooshmand yet. Between shoots, she would still take on voice-over and events jobs. Subsisting on acting alone, especially as an independent artist, is becoming progressively harder, this she admits. She’s still in survival mode. But there’s a maxim she keeps close in moments of doubt and struggle: “Faith can give you wings.”

It was faith that allowed her to manifest working with Jadaone and sending an audition tape without knowing what it was for. It was faith when Mabesa believed she could lead an entire production. It was still faith when she pushed through the audition for Ria, despite a body on the brink of collapse.

And despite having her most prolific and breakout year, what Hooshmand ascertains is that she won’t just jump from one project to the next, a glaring contrast to an industry that would often capitalize on momentum.
It has been her default to connect with the people she works with and genuinely care for them. “Everything has a reason,” she said. “It’s either to teach you something or to teach them something.”
To that end, she disclosed declining major offers from big corporations a couple of times. “I wanted to try to pave a new path for myself,” she explained.

She’s well aware that it’s a stubborn principle, one that her friend and fellow actor Maris Racal said would prove difficult for her career. “But I wanted to show that it’s possible,” Hooshmand insisted, somehow echoing the worldview of her character, Ria.

As she has come to realize early on, everything eventually accumulates. “If you work hard, if you are kind to people, if you show up, organically you will find work, you will find the right people.” – Rappler.com
