articles.title: Decision clearing path for Russia to join world juniors in Alberta is 'very unwelcome,' minister says
articles.summary: Canada's foreign affairs minister says the decision to let Russia back into the ice hockey world championships came as a "great disappointment" on Friday, as the country's ongoing invasion of Ukraine…

image.caption: Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand, seen in Toronto last month, says the government is still assessing the ruling from the Court of Arbitration for Sport that will allow Russian athletes to compete at the hockey world championships. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada

Canada's foreign affairs minister says the decision to let Russia back into the ice hockey world championships came as a "great disappointment" on Friday, as the country's ongoing invasion of Ukraine stretches toward its fifth year.
Anita Anand says 'all options are on the table' for Canada before hockey championship

Minister Anita Anand said the Canadian government is still assessing the ruling from the Court of Arbitration for Sport, but said she was "not comfortable" with potentially allowing a Russian team to attend this year's World Junior Ice Hockey Championships in Alberta.

"Make no mistake, this is a very unwelcome decision given the geopolitical situation, given the actions of Russia," Anand told CBC's Power & Politics. "All options are on the table and I will say, again, I greet this decision with great disappointment."
'Focus on the substance' of Canada and EU's partnership, not the name: Anand

items: Russia is back in the hockey world championships after sports court ruling

blocks.text: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) cleared the path on Friday for Russia to return to the ice hockey world championships, overturning an exclusion in place since the country invaded Ukraine in early 2022.

The court's ruling overturned International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) decisions, which had banned Russia and Belarus from international tournaments since Feb. 28, 2022. The federation, while disappointed with the decision, said on Friday it would "act in accordance" with the ruling.
This year's world juniors are scheduled for Dec. 26, 2026, to Jan. 5, 2027, in Alberta in Red Deer and Edmonton.
Ministers boycott group photo with Russian counterpart at G20

Also on Friday, the United States cancelled a traditional group photo the G20 Foreign Ministers Meeting in Atlanta after several European officials threatened to boycott the picture over the inclusion of Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

In her interview, Anand said she was going to miss the picture because she was on a flight to the Canada–EU summit in Montreal, but, had she been there, she said she would've joined her fellow ministers in skipping the picture in protest.
"It is not my preference at all to be in a picture with Sergey Lavrov," she said. She added that she ultimately sat across from the Russian minister once meetings got underway.
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, centre, attends the G20 Foreign Ministers Meeting in Atlanta on Friday. (Megan Varner/Pool/The Associated Press)
From her seat, Anand said she looked the Russian minister "straight in the eye" and told him Russian's ongoing attacks in Ukraine are "absolutely reprehensible and contrary to international law."

Some G20 countries had already expressed concern at the U.S. having invited Russia to the meetings, especially after U.S. President Donald Trump drove his administration's relationship with Ukraine to deeper lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance.
The Canadian government has expressed solidarity with Ukraine from the outset and the two countries declared a 100-year partnership last month.

articles.title: He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
articles.summary: Thailand has prosecuted 294 people since 2020 under its lèse majesté law, with sentences going up to 50 years.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Arnon Nampa dressed as Harry Potter at the protest in August 2020
ByJonathan Head
South East Asia correspondentReporting fromBangkok
Even before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.
The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.
One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.

This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.

On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lèse majesté law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.
This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending.
"To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."

blocks.caption: Image caption, A drawing by Arnon Nampa's 10-year-old daughter showing her father in prison

blocks.text: Image source, Arnon Nampa's family
A drawing by Arnon Nampa's 10-year-old daughter showing her father in prison

The past six years have seen the most extensive use of lèse majesté in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.

Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".

Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."

In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions.

"If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lèse majesté under Section 112."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Arnon at a protest in 2023

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Arnon at a protest in 2023
From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son.
"Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children,

The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom."
Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.
Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.

But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Arnon's family, drawn by his daughter, titled "heading to court". Her mum is carrying a poster that says, "Free my dad"

blocks.text: Arnon's family, drawn by his daughter, titled "heading to court". Her mum is carrying a poster that says, "Free my dad"

The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.
That changed on 3 August 2020.

That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.

In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.

In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.

At the time, the use of the lèse majesté law had been suspended for three years. Sources close to the palace have in the past acknowledged that the negative publicity generated by lèse majesté convictions might do more harm than good.
But the protests forced a hasty reassessment. From the end of 2020 prosecutions under the law restarted and accelerated. Dozens of young activists have fled into exile to avoid being jailed.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Arnon's reunion with his family, as drawn by his daughter

blocks.text: Arnon's reunion with his family, as drawn by his daughter
One of them is Supitcha "Melinn" Chailom. The 24-year-old from Chiang Mai in northern Thailand lives in Montreal, a fugitive from four 112 charges which have been filed against her.
She was an 18-year-old school girl when she stood up and made a speech at a protest in Chiang Mai University, just three weeks after Arnon Nampa's call for reform of the monarchy.

A local photographer captured the moment she raised her hand in the three-finger Hunger Games salute, eliciting loud cheers from the crowd. It became one of the defining images of the protests, and propelled Melinn to nationwide fame.

She travelled up and down the country as one of the leading voices in the movement, demanding changes to Thailand's old-fashioned education system, conducting polls on what people thought of the monarchy.
"I love playing games, and I dreamed of being a game designer," she told me from Canada. But her parents did not approve.
"I felt that, as a young person, I could not question, or have a discussion with people older than me. The monarchy gave me the same vibe."

In November 2020 Melinn joined a protest in the southern city of Hat Yai, where she gave a speech comparing the royal treatment given to the king's dog with that of ordinary people. Nine months later the police delivered a summons to her home charging her with lèse majesté.

"It was a shock. I wasn't expecting it because I only talked about the dog. It was during Covid when the police came to my home with the summons, so they knew my parents would be there with me. They tried to stay calm, but I nearly lost my mind."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Melinn doing the three-finger salute in August 2020

blocks.text: Image source, Goodmondayshoot
Melinn doing the three-finger salute in August 2020
Her family tried to persuade her to co-operate with the authorities, to admit her wrongdoing. But Melinn refused.

She joined a movement calling itself Thalu Wang, which translates as "breaking through the palace". Instead of giving speeches, they came up with stunts like holding polls on the street, asking people what they thought of royal motorcades holding up the traffic, or whether they believed the monarchy had too much power.
"We knew the risks, but we thought it would be safer just conducting a poll. It turns out it was not."

She was given two more lèse majesté charges in 2022, and detained before being released on bail. She had to wear an electronic monitor on her ankle and was barred from leaving her home between 4pm and 6am. Her parents were forced to sign a document promising to inform on her. She was facing decades in jail.
Melinn decided she had no choice. With a friend she fled Thailand and eventually got asylum in Canada.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A painting by Arnon's daughter titled "my dad's feelings"

blocks.text: A painting by Arnon's daughter titled "my dad's feelings"

Article 112 is on paper just a law, like any other, passed by Thai parliament, which can, theoretically, be amended by elected MPs. In fact it has been amended in the past, notably in 1976 when the punishment for breaking it was increased to between three and 15 years in prison.

But today the Constitutional Court has decreed that the law itself, like the institution it protects, is untouchable. The reformist Move Forward party - the successor of Future Forward - was dissolved in 2024, and its leader banned from politics, merely for proposing that the punishments be less harsh. And the courts make it very difficult for those charged under it to defend themselves.

"In many cases, like the one against Arnon Nampa, prosecutors accuse the defendant of lying about the monarchy," says Chaimaneekarakate, the lawyer. "But when we ask the judge to subpoena documents or witnesses who could show the truth of what the defendant says, the judge refuses to do it. When one lawyer protested against the court deciding that the trial would be held in secret, she was warned by the judge to be quiet or face a contempt of court charge."
He says judges sometimes criticise the young activists over their alleged actions even before the trial has started.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Arnon has been writing letters to his children since he was jailed three years ago

blocks.text: Image source, Arnon Nampa
Arnon has been writing letters to his children since he was jailed three years ago

As the one who ignited the debate about the monarchy Arnon appears to be getting the harshest punishment. Despite the formidable odds stacked against him he still prepares carefully for every court appearance, taking part in his own defence and helping other inmates with theirs.
This isn't easy; he is not allowed to bring any of his written notes, and must memorise all his arguments.
The judges object to him playing the part of a lawyer in his regulation-brown prison shorts, his feet bare and shackled. But it does give him an opportunity to see his family.

The letters he writes are the only other way he stays in touch with them. He may spend his entire life in prison. He wants his children to know him, and to understand, when they are older, why he chose to challenge the system and lose his freedom.

"Since the first day that we made up our mind to take up this mission, we knew of the dangers. Speaking the truth is not difficult. What is difficult is speaking a forbidden truth. I remember well that on the evening of 3 August 2020, after speaking at the Harry Potter event, I felt very good, content, and relieved to have finally begun speaking about the truth, in public," he wrote to his family last year.

Earlier this year, he wrote: "Living here is a struggle. But it is just a dot in the bigger picture of our movement's struggle. We must play a part in writing our own history. Become a drop of water that will one day become an ocean."

articles.title: Poland: Protesters clash with police over sacked court chief
articles.summary: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk defended the firing of top court President Bogdan Swieczkowski as a move to "restore the rule of law."

image.caption: Donald Tusk's center-left governing alliance had vowed to reverse controversial PiS judicial reformsImage: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

blocks.text: Protesters gathered outside Poland's Constitutional Court on Friday night, with authorities sending police to the scene to secure the court's grounds.

It all comes after a statement appeared on the top court's website saying President Bogdan Swieczkowski and his deputy had been suspended for one month. Fellow judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska will lead the institution during this period.
According to Warsaw police, officers responded to one judge who alerted them to possible threats to the safety of judges and staff.
Tusk vows to 'restore rule of law'
Swieczkowski is one of a slew of politically aligned judges who were appointed by the right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS), which governed Poland from 2015 to 2023.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk backed the move in a post on X.
"Restoring the rule of law is our duty," Tusk said.
"After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way," he added.

blocks.caption: Officers responded to a judge who alerted them to possible threats to the safety of judges and staffImage: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

blocks.text: When Tusk's center-left alliance took over after the 2023 parliamentary election, the group announced it would reverse controversial PiS government reforms in the judiciary.
President cancels trip abroad
Right-wing Polish President Karol Nawrocki reacted to the situation by canceling a planned trip to Senegal.
"At a moment like this, the president must be in Poland," Nawrocki said.
But in recent months, Nawrocki had refused to swear in five top court judges nominated by parliament.
When these judges instead took their oath before parliament, Swieczkowski had denied them access to the building.

articles.title: Retired Michigan teacher released from Russian prison believed he would never be freed
articles.summary:
Stephen Hubbard said that only when he was being taken from Moscow to St Petersburg did he believe he was ‘going somewhere’

In his first comments since recently being

blocks.text: In his first comments since recently being released from a Russian prison, a retired Michigan teacher said he only believed he would be freed when he got new clothes.

Stephen Hubbard, 74, remarked on Friday that he had heard many times previously that he would be released – but never really trusted what he was told, adopting a philosophy of “seeing is believing” and “actions speak louder than words”.

“Only when they started giving me new clothes and leading me to the exit of the prison,” Hubbard said in his first public remarks since his 21 October release, which came during a visit at the White House with Donald Trump, “I went out and I saw the car, and I was accompanied by a couple of Russians, then I believed, finally believed, on the drive from Moscow to St Petersburg, ‘I’m really going somewhere.’”

Hubbard had been behind bars for more than four years on charges that he fought as a mercenary in Ukraine, which Russia invaded in February 2022. His legal team has denied the Russian accusations and said he was not involved in any military activity.
Trump has previously said that he had asked Russian leader Vladimir Putin to free Hubbard – and that the US did not have to release anyone in return.
“He was somebody I wanted to get back,” the US president said as he hosted Hubbard on Friday in the Oval Office.
The White House allowed a limited pool of journalists into Trump’s meeting with Hubbard, allowing primarily news photographers and a television crew.

Many in the international community perceived Hubbard’s release to be Russia’s latest maneuver to bring Trump closer to Putin’s position on the war in Ukraine. It also offered Trump a diplomatic victory ahead of the 3 November midterm elections, when his Republican party is expected to lose seats in Congress.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Democratic lawmakers demand ICE data on detainee miscarriages
articles.summary:
ICE failed to record data on miscarriages suffered by immigrants in its custody between October 2025 and June 2026

US lawmakers are urgently demanding that

blocks.text: US lawmakers are urgently demanding that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) disclose how many pregnant immigrants have experienced miscarriages, stillbirths and pregnancy-related hospitalizations while in the its custody, after the agency admitted it lost count last year.

US representatives sent the request following a recent Guardian investigation revealing that the Trump administration is detaining a record number of pregnant women and teens, and at the same has lost track of how many suffered miscarriages.

In a letter to ICE’s acting director, David Venturella, Democratic representatives Brittany Pettersen, Joyce Beatty and Robin Kelly also asked the immigration enforcement agency to explain what – if any – steps have been taken to recover any missing data about these cases.

Government documents obtained by the Guardian found that ICE had placed more pregnant immigrants in detention last fall and winter than at any time over the previous year. The agency recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration, the documents found, but the agency has no data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025.

Detained pregnant women said that they were struggling to access routine and emergency medical care. Medical experts told the Guardian that lapses in care both during pregnancy and during and after miscarriage could escalate treatable conditions into life-threatening emergencies.

In their letter, the representatives also cite a 2021 directive instructing ICE to wholly avoid detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants “unless release is prohibited by law or exceptional circumstances exist” – and ask the agency to clarify on what grounds it is detaining pregnant immigrants. The directive also requires ICE to closely monitor and document the health of all pregnant people in its custody, and continuously evaluate whether it is medically advisable to keep them detained.

“ICE’s inability to follow agency directives, provide adequate medical care and maintain accurate records of pregnancy-related medical outcomes is unacceptable,” the lawmakers wrote in their letter, which was cosigned by 64 other representatives.

In an interview, Pettersen said it was “deeply concerning” that ICE had failed to account for a full year of pregnancy outcomes. “I’m just devastated for the people who have gone through this, who’ve lost pregnancies unnecessarily, who have been left without the medical care that they need after miscarrying,” she said. “It’s hard to imagine how we are ever going to right these wrongs.”

In internal agency documents, ICE said it had no data on miscarriages because the agency changed medical billing providers in October. The agency’s medical claims processing has been delayed for months. Immigration attorneys and former government officials told said it was odd, but plausible, that ICE was keeping track of miscarriages solely via its medical billing provider.

In response to follow-up questions about its tracking practices after 3 October 2025, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, first said that the agency was tracking miscarriages in monthly reports. But later, the spokesperson confirmed what was in the ICE internal documents – the agency does not have data on miscarriages between October 2025 through June 2026.
after newsletter promotion

The DHS did not confirm to the Guardian whether it had received the letter from Congress members. “Claims that any pregnant detainees are receiving subprime care are FALSE,” an agency spokesperson said.

In their letter, lawmakers asked ICE’s acting director to detail when “ICE leadership first became aware of concerns regarding miscarriage reporting and deficiencies in agency tracking systems”. They gave the agency until 6 November to respond.
Prior to the Guardian’s reporting, the agency had never acknowledged that it had lost count of miscarriages – not even when US senators asked the agency for the data.

The Guardian filed a Freedom of Information Act request and then filed suit in collaboration with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press to obtain data on the number of pregnant people in ICE detention, and the health outcomes for this population.

Javits Frimpong, 15, was being bullied at school before he was shot and killed in the Bronx on Thursday, his father says

A teenage boy from Ghana was chased down and fatally shot Thursday…

blocks.text: A teenage boy from Ghana was chased down and fatally shot Thursday morning on his way to school in the Bronx.

The New York City police department (NYPD) received a report on Thursday morning about a shooting near Corona Park in the Bronx, a police spokesperson said on Friday. At about 9.24am, responding officers found Javits Frimpong, 15, with a gunshot wound to his stomach.

Javits was transported to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead. Police have not made any arrests and an investigation is ongoing as authorities search for three teenage boys in connection to the shooting.

Surveillance footage reportedly captured Javits running, as a person wearing all black trailed behind. Another angle of video footage appeared to show masked individuals in dark clothing fleeing the site of the shooting.
The deadly attack has rocked the Bronx’s Claremont neighborhood and the city’s west African community.
“I lost him,” the teenager’s father, Thomas Frimpong, told reporters on Thursday. “I don’t know what to do now.”

The fatal shooting came as Javits marked one year of being in New York after arriving from Ghana, Frimpong said. Frimpong described his son as “clever” and “quiet”. Javits was being bullied at the DreamYard preparatory school, according to Frimpong.
Frimpong said the high school’s principal, who could not be reached for comment by phone or email, informed him recently that two students were suspended for harassing Javits, he said.
An NYPD spokesperson declined to comment Friday on whether the reports of bullying were related to the attack.

Ghana’s minister of foreign affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, condemned the attack in a Friday statement. “We will pursue justice and we will make sure that those who did this do not get away with it.”

“Just one year ago, Javits arrived in the United States from Ghana to reunite with his father and begin a new chapter of his life. Like so many Ghanaian immigrant families, his family came together in America with hopes of greater opportunity, security, and a promising future,” the Ghana diaspora public affairs collective, a US-based non-profit, also said in a Friday statement.
“That future has now been violently taken away.”

blocks.text: PITX: Bicol-bound bus trips continue despite Mayon eruption
Despite Mayon Volcano's eruption on Friday morning, bus trips bound for Bicol from the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) remain uninterrupted.

In a "24 Oras" report by Jonathan Andal on Friday, PITX said six out of every 10 buses bound for Bicol were already fully booked. However, walk-in passengers could still be accommodated on ordinary and air-conditioned buses with available seats.
While some Bicol-bound passengers expressed concern over Mayon's eruption, they still pushed through with their trips. Others, meanwhile, were unaware of the volcanic activity.
“Nakakapagalala kasi wala po kaming balita talaga na pumutok pala yung bulkan. Hangga’t mayroon pong bumabyahe, parang tutuloy po kami,” said Daisy Belga, a passenger bound for Albay.
(It's worrying because we had no idea that the volcano had erupted. But as long as buses are still operating, we will push through with our trip.)
“Kinakabahan, pero mostly kasi tagilid naman kami, [sa] Polangui. Medyo gilid man pero abot kami ng ashfall,” added Virgie Magalona, another passenger bound for Albay.
(I'm nervous, but we're somewhat off to the side in Polangui. Even though we're not directly in the affected area, ashfall can still reach us.)
In Andal's report, a bus company said its drivers traveling to Bicol had reported no problems along their routes. However, driver Lito Rodriguez said he would remain cautious.
“Medyo delikado. Magpapa-ano na lang, magpapababa muna ng abo,” Rodriguez said.
(It's somewhat dangerous. I'll just wait for the ash to settle first.)
PITX said buses with online reservation systems were already fully booked, but many buses without online booking options continued to operate even without full passenger loads.
Since October 25, PITX has recorded more than one million passengers.
The terminal's security personnel have also confiscated hundreds of prohibited items, including pointed objects and flammable materials.
Passengers heading to their hometowns brought various types of luggage, with some even traveling with their pets.
PITX said pets are generally allowed on buses with their owners, provided they comply with the requirements.
“Usually ina-allow ng mga buses natin. Dapat po may cage, vaccination card at siyempre diaper po,” PITX Deputy Spokesperson Kolyn Gervacio-Calbasa said.
(Our buses generally allow pets, provided they are in cages and have vaccination cards and diapers.)
Meanwhile, large crowds of passengers have also started gathering at the Five Star bus terminal in Cubao, Quezon City, with some trips bound for Cagayan already fully booked.

Victory Liner has increased the number of trips from Manila to Baguio to 250, up from 150, as it expects passenger volume on the route to double to 10,000 starting October 31. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/VBL, GMA News
Manila Port tightens safety measures for Undas 2026 amid passenger surge
Tighter safety measures are being implemented at the Manila Port amid this year’s exodus for Undas, following a RoRo vessel that listed to its right in Real, Quezon, on Friday morning.
In a "24 Oras report by Ian Cruz on Friday, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) conducted thorough inspections at the port to ensure that cargo on the vessels is properly secured.

“Binigyan na po natin ng instruction ang ating mga inspector na busisiin nang maigi ‘yung mga cargo lalong-lalo na itong mga rolling cargo o mga sasakyan na sakay ng vessel, na siguraduhing nakatali at maayos dahil konting galaw lang po ng barko maaari po ‘yang mag-move at ma-outbalance ang barko pwede po siyang tumagilid,” Coast Guard Station Manila Deputy Commander P/Lt. Luther Quela said.

(We have already instructed our inspectors to meticulously check cargo—especially rolling cargo or vehicles on board the vessel—to ensure they are properly tied down and secured, because even a slight movement of the ship can cause them to shift, unbalance the vessel, and cause it to list.)
Several passengers at the port chose to travel by ship to save on fare and bring more luggage.
“Ang ticket namin for 3 pax nasa 12 [thousand] eh. On the way pa lang,” said Fatima Belarmino, a passenger bound for Cebu.
She added that traveling by airplane would require a budget of P10,000 per person.
Meanwhile, couple Rosanna Layson and Rick Moulton chose to take a ship so they could bring three carts of baggage to Palawan.
“Sa barko madadala namin lahat ng gamit namin sa bahay, durabox, mga chair. Hindi naman namin madadala lahat yan sa airplane,” Layson said.
(On a ship, we can bring all our household items, plastic storage boxes, and chairs. We wouldn't be able to bring all of that on an airplane.)
“Plane is quicker, that’s for sure, but it will be an interesting experience,” Moulton added.
Passenger turnout this year was lower compared to last year, according to the North Port manager. On Friday, passenger volume reached over 1,100.
At the Batangas Port, passenger numbers were also low. From midnight to 4 a.m. on Friday, only over 2,100 passengers arrived, alongside 358 rolling cargoes.
On Thursday, passengers departing from the Batangas pier reached 7,000, compared to 12,000 passengers in 2025.

“Matumal pa ang pagdating ng pasahero ngayon, compared noong isang taon. Nagmahal talaga ang pamasahe. Mauunawaan naman natin ang mga shipping lines because alam naman natin na mataas na ang presyo ng produktong petrolyo,” Batangas Port Manager Aurora Mendoza said.
(Passenger arrivals are still slow today compared to last year. Fares have genuinely increased. We can understand the shipping lines because we know that petroleum product prices are high.)
The PCG reminded the public that shipping companies do not allow the boarding of electric or hybrid vehicles on ships as part of heightened safety precautions. –Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Alaska prosecutor investigates alleged Democratic plot to confuse voters with second Dan Sullivan
articles.summary: Mary Peltola denies knowledge as party accused of recruiting spoiler candidate with same name as sitting Republican
articles.byline: Lucy Campbell, Robert Mackey and agencies

blocks.text: The top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed on Friday the existence of a criminal and a civil investigation into an alleged scheme by Democrats to confuse voters by recruiting a spoiler candidate on the ballot for US Senate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent, senator Dan Sullivan.

Speaking at a news conference in Anchorage on Friday, US attorney Michael Heyman cited reporting by the New York Times which suggested that the Senate campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola and national Democrats had, in his words, “orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up Daniel J Sullivan as a sham candidate”.
Both Dan Sullivans – one a Republican senator and the other a retired schoolteacher with no prior political experience – qualified for the ballot.
“We are taking that extremely seriously,” Heyman said.

“This new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska,” he added. “As we speak, law enforcement around the country are taking investigative steps with respect to a criminal investigation on these matters.”

Separately, the Department of Justice on Friday asked a federal judge to issue a preliminary ⁠injunction ​that would ‌block ‌Alaska from ‌certifying its Senate election result if the incumbent senator loses to Peltola due to the presence of Daniel J Sullivan on the ballot.

Heyman would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into. It is highly unusual for federal prosecutors to confirm the existence of an open criminal investigation, much less discuss it publicly.
“The civil lawsuit is publicly faced, and is focused on preserving the ballots,” Heyman said, referring to a Department of Justice suit filed last week.
A day earlier, Peltola denied any prior knowledge of the alleged effort, telling supporters in Juneau, Alaska’s capital: “I am not interested in tricking voters.”

“I just want to clear the air,” the Democratic Senate candidate said on Thursday at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about.”

Peltola is running against Dan Sullivan, the two-term US senator. A person familiar with the matter told the Associated Press that subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after the New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J Sullivan Jr as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters.

The race is considered one of the most important contests of next week’s midterm elections, and will be key to determining control of the Senate. Alaska is one of a handful of states with Senate races this year that Democrats are targeting as they try to win back a majority in the chamber, where they hold 47 seats to the Republican party’s 53, and recent polls have shown Peltola in the lead.
More subpoenas were expected, according to the person who spoke to the Associated Press. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the number of them were immediately clear.

Republicans have condemned the presence in the race of two candidates named Dan Sullivan, calling the newcomer a ploy by Democrats to cost the incumbent re-election by splitting the GOP candidate’s supporters.

Before the August primary, election authorities in the state attempted to disqualify the other Dan Sullivan, but the state supreme court ruled that he could appear on the ballot. Together with Sullivan and Peltola, the challenger was one of the top four vote-getters in the non-partisan primary.
after newsletter promotion
On the general election ballot, the senator will be listed as “Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent” and the challenger “Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.”

Since the New York Times published its report, Mike Dunleavy, Alaska’s Republican governor, separately announced plans to launch a criminal investigation, saying the story revealed “disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates – including one with the same name as an incumbent US senator – to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes”.

“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the report “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.
Donald Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate if she won the election.
“Well, you’re going to have to see what happens,” the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. “It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”
Later, as he rallied for Darline Graham, a Republican senator, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted”.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
articles.summary: The American-made interceptors are the only effective weapon for downing Russia's ballistic missiles.

blocks.text: The US has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks, after Kyiv said deliveries had been delayed in recent months.
The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly urged the US to speed up deliveries of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.
The latest move comes just days after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump, with the US president saying it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to try to end the war with Russia.

In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".
It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".
The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".
Zelensky said earlier this week that his country had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies.
And in a Telegram post late on Friday, the Ukrainian president reported that earlier in the day Russian ballistic missiles had struck two of the country's regions.
"They continue to carry out terrorist strikes against our cities," he said.
Zelensky has recently admitted that Ukraine was running critically low on Patriots, as Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.

It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.
Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.
In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriots - three weeks after offering the country such a right.

articles.title: Canadian Crime Stoppers Association advises chapters to accept tips by phone only
articles.summary: The Canadian Crime Stoppers Association is advising its local chapters to solely accept tips by telephone instead of online, it said in a statement to CBC News on Friday.

blocks.text: Investigates
The Canadian Crime Stoppers Association is advising its local chapters to solely accept tips by telephone instead of online, it said in a statement to CBC News on Friday.
Public asked to call 222-TIPS to submit tips anonymously
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 30, 2026 5:54 PM EDT | Last Updated: 36 minutes ago
The Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) is advising its local chapters to solely accept tips by telephone instead of online, it said in a statement to CBC News on Friday.

The "interim telephone-only approach … will allow participating local programs to receive tips without using Navigate360’s P3 platform," reads the statement, referring to the third-party U.S. company's tip management platform that suffered a massive data breach in March.

It appears to be a shift for the not-for-profit organization, which had previously issued guidance to local programs that if asked about the breach by members of the public, they should express their confidence in Navigate360's security improvements and say the platform "remains secure and appropriate for continued use."

In the Friday statement, the CCSA asked that the public now call 222-TIPS to submit tips anonymously. For programs that have been paused, there will be local announcements about when telephone reporting will resume, it said.
"Local programs will keep new information under their control and share it securely with law enforcement," reads the statement from CCSA president David J. Forster.

The extent of the breach was revealed in a CBC investigation published last week, which found that over 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years had been hacked.
To date, more than 40 local Crime Stoppers chapters and police agencies in five provinces have temporarily paused their intake of anonymous tips or their partnerships with the organization.
More to come.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Valérie Ouellet is a bilingual senior reporter with CBC’s Investigative Unit in Toronto. Her data-driven stories on women’s health, medical devices, international students and the correctional system have earned numerous awards and accolades, including the St. Clair Balfour Fellowship at Massey College and the CAJ Data Journalism Award. She also teaches data journalism and mentors reporters across Canada. Since joining CBC/Radio-Canada in 2010, she has reported from Saskatchewan, Ontario and Quebec in both official languages. You can contact her with tips to valerie.ouellet@cbc.ca.

The head of a Toronto real estate group says his family is traumatized and recovering after they were attacked in a violent home invasion in the Bridle Path neighbourhood Thursday morning.
Toronto real estate CEO David Morton says his family members were shot, attacked with hammer

David Morton, CEO of MAC Group, said three members of his family are recovering in hospital after they were shot during the home invasion. All four members of the family were also attacked with a hammer, he said in a statement issued Friday.
"It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home," he said.
"No family should ever have to experience this. People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives."

items: 4 hospitalized as Toronto police investigate home invasion, shooting at Bridle Path home

blocks.text: On Thursday, Toronto police said they responded to reports of a "violent home invasion" and shooting at a home on Hyde Park Circle near Bayview Avenue and Lawrence Avenue E., around 3:43 a.m.

Police said three suspects, armed with handguns and a hammer, forced their way into the home through a rear entrance and attacked four adults in the home — a father, mother and their two adult daughters.
Two of the family members have life-altering injuries, police said.
Toronto police continue to investigate and are searching for three suspects.

Police are also urging anyone with information, dashcam footage or doorbell camera video to contact them.

articles.title: U.S. charges 5 more Canadians with voter fraud offences amid Trump administration crackdown
articles.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice says charges have been laid against five more Canadians for voting fraud-related offences, the latest in a flurry of similar prosecutions ahead of next week's midterm…

image.caption: The two women pictured are among at least 20 Canadians either charged with or sentenced for voting fraud-related offences in the U.S. this year. (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement/U.S. Department of Homeland Security)

blocks.text: World·New

The U.S. Department of Justice says charges have been laid against five more Canadians for voting fraud-related offences, the latest in a flurry of similar prosecutions ahead of next week's midterm elections.
At least 20 Canadians now charged or sentenced in U.S. election integrity investigations this year

According to a tally compiled by CBC News, at least 20 Canadians have now been either charged or sentenced in the U.S. this year in federal election integrity investigations. Most charges have been filed since last month, with allegations typically dating back several years.

The five latest cases were announced in a series of news releases Thursday and Friday from U.S. attorney's offices in Missouri, Tennessee, North Carolina and Wisconsin. They all involve Canadians living in the U.S. — most of them listed as lawful permanent residents — accused of falsely claiming citizenship to cast a ballot, or illegally voting in a past election.
The defendants are between 58 and 68 years old, according to the Department of Justice.

items: Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown as U.S. accuses Canada of election interference

blocks.text: "The right to vote is fundamental to American citizenship and a cornerstone of our republic," Dan Bishop, the U.S. attorney for the Middle District of North Carolina, said in a statement.
Bishop said the recent charges "serve notice that those who violate our election laws, including non-citizens who register and vote, will be investigated and prosecuted."

A 69-year-old Canadian woman charged with 'illegal voting by an alien' was arrested after dark while in her housecoat, according to this image released by U.S. authorities. (U.S. Department of Homeland Security)

U.S. federal prosecutors and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) — a branch of Immigration and Customs Enforcement — have in recent weeks repeatedly highlighted their efforts to crack down on voter fraud.
"Anyone who unlawfully votes will be found and brought to justice!" HSI said Friday in a post on X.
U.S. authorities have announced similar charges against citizens of several other countries including Australia, Colombia, Cuba, Jamaica and the United Kingdom.

items: U.S. officials accuse Canada of midterm meddling — but Trump has endorsed foreign candidates

blocks.text: The efforts align with U.S. President Donald Trump's long-running false claims of widespread voter fraud in federal elections.
"The timing tells us why it's likely they're doing this," said David Becker, executive director of the non-partisan Center for Election Innovation and Research, in a recent interview.
He insisted what little non-citizen voting occurs in the U.S. has not affected the outcomes of elections.
Canadians sternly warned to stay out of U.S. elections as arrests ramp up
"This is likely an attempt to try to sow doubts about the election, in advance of an election in which the president and his administration might fear the voters might reject them," Becker said.
Last week, the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa said in a statement Canadians account for the "second highest total of prosecutions for fraudulent or illegal voting of any country."

items: U.S. 'monitoring' Canada for signs of midterm election interference, ambassador says

blocks.text: The embassy pointedly warned "all Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence U.S. elections in any way. Americans decide America's elections."

articles.title: Canada finding 'solutions' on EU carbon tariff threat: Carney
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says Ottawa made progress on a trade irritant with the European Union — a pending carbon tariff on energy intensive Canadian goods.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks to the media during the closing press conference at the EU-Canada summit in Montreal on Friday. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
Prime Minister Mark Carney says Ottawa made progress on a trade irritant with the European Union — a pending carbon tariff on energy intensive Canadian goods.
Ambassador says the EU will recognize Canada's carbon price
Prime Minister Mark Carney says Ottawa has made progress on a trade irritant with the European Union — a carbon tariff on energy intensive Canadian exports.

At the closing news conference for the Canada-EU summit in Montreal, Carney said there are "common solutions" to resolving the carbon import levy on Canadian products such as iron ore, steel, aluminum, cement and other goods.
Following up on Carney's remarks to a reporter's question, EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she couldn't have answered it better on what she called "trade irritants."

items: Carney says, unequivocally, Canada seeking to become the EU's 1st associate member

blocks.text: The EU's carbon border adjustment mechanism, or CBAM, is currently being applied at a low level and will ramp up to full implementation in 2034. It's meant to encourage exporters from around the world, not just Canada, to lower the planet-warming emissions created when producing their industrial goods.

CBC News reported ahead of the summit that Ottawa's diplomats were concerned about not only the carbon tariff that would be imposed but the cost of compliance. Canadian exporters would need to assess, report and verify the amount of embodied carbon in products.

items: Canada facing carbon tariff threat from European Union: internal documents

blocks.text: CBC obtained an internal document ahead of the summit, which shed light on Ottawa's concerns. Global Affairs estimated $2.8 billion worth of goods annually are exposed to the carbon import levy — primarily on metals that are already affected by U.S tariffs.
Those figures are averages based on data between 2021 and 2024, meaning exposure could be higher as Canadian goods seek new buyers to avoid U.S. tariffs.
The memo also states Canada is not exempt from the carbon tariff even with Canada's national price on carbon and its decade-old trade deal with the European Union.
Canada's ambassador-designate to the EU, Jonathan Wilkinson, spoke with CBC's Power & Politics and confirmed diplomatic talks are heading in the right direction but not resolved.

Wilkinson said "the problem" Ottawa had with the European carbon border mechanism is it did not acknowledge Canadian producers were doing their part to reduce their greenhouse gas footprint by paying an industrial carbon price.
"We made enormous progress addressing those issues," Wilkinson told host David Cochrane. "They [the EU] will recognize our carbon price."

John Hannaford, personal representative of the prime minister to the EU, left, and Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada's ambassador-designate to the EU, arrive at a news conference at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Sept. 17. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
It's not clear how much credit producers will get for paying Canada's carbon price, but Wilkinson said "there's a bit of work" still to do.
"Effectively, it needs to be in place by, I think, September or October of 2027. So there's some time," Wilkinson said.
Wilkinson said Canada has a competitive advantage compared with other countries, like the United States, who don't have a carbon price and will likely face a full tariff from the E.U.
The update from the Carney government comes as the Liberals were under new pressure from the Conservatives to resolve the issue.

"Prime Minister Mark Carney has spent months talking up Canada’s relationship with the European Union. But to date, has failed to eliminate this threat to Canadian businesses," read a statement from the Conservatives.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

David Thurton is a senior reporter in CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. He covers daily politics in the nation’s capital and specializes in environment and energy policy. Born in Canada but raised in Trinidad and Tobago, he’s moved around more times than he can count. He’s worked for CBC in several provinces and territories, including Alberta and the Northwest Territories. He can be reached at david.thurton@cbc.ca

articles.title: Alberta separatist Jeff Rath kicked out of governing United Conservative Party
articles.summary: In an email, the party's executive director said Rath had "made clear" he did "not support" the party.

image.caption: Jeffrey Rath, co-founder of the Alberta Prosperity Project, speaks to journalists at a referendum watch party in Edmonton, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (John Ulan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
In an email, the party's executive director said Rath had "made clear" he did "not support" the party.
In an email, the party said he had 'made clear' he did 'not support' party
Separatist leader Jeff Rath, who rose to prominence in the lead-up to the Alberta referendum in his white cowboy hat, has had his membership revoked by the governing United Conservative Party.

In an email sent to Rath on Thursday and viewed by CBC News, Dustin Van Vugt, the party's executive director, said that Rath's "words and actions have made clear" that he does not support the party or its objectives.
"Your public conduct in relation to our party and leader has not met the basic standard of decency we expect of our members when they disagree or otherwise."
His membership was revoked immediately, Van Vugt wrote.
In a phone call, Rath said he knew why he was being singled out.
"Because I'm a very loud and effective critic of Danielle Smith," he said.
"She obviously does not want free speech in the party."
Rath said he also received an email from the UCP notifying him the party had refunded the $239 he paid in order to attend next month's AGM.
Rath and Smith have publicly sparred over their differing views on Alberta’s place in Confederation, and their debates have occasionally veered into more personal territory.

Earlier this week, Rath accused Smith of colluding with federalist leader Thomas Lukaszuk in a text exchange he posted online. When NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi questioned Smith about it, the premier noted Rath’s prior financial contributions to the Opposition party.
Speaking to reporters Friday, Smith confirmed the party's executive director had pulled Rath's membership.
"He’s never supported me ... He never supported me during the leadership, he never supported me in my time in office, and he certainly doesn’t support me now," she said.

"That’s irrelevant," she added. "What is relevant is that he has said publicly things like he wants to come to the AGM to turn the UCP into an independence party. And we are not an independence party."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alex Boyd is a senior reporter based in Calgary, interested in politics, provincial affairs and misinformation. She is a former national and investigative reporter for the Toronto Star. Reach her at alex.boyd@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Canadian PM Mark Carney discusses talks with the EU, overdependence on the US and how to deal with Donald Trump in a DW interview.
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney tells DW that Canada is seeking closer EU ties to "diversify and deepen" partnerships beyond the Americas. Despite German pushback, he said he favors the all-new term…

image.caption: Carney told DW that in 'many cases' there could be scope for deeper Canada-EU cooperation than between Canada and the USImage: Dmytro Rusanov/DW

blocks.text: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke to DW on Friday after talks in Montreal with European Union leaders seeking to hammer out details of a new, closer partnership between Canada and the EU.

Amid difficult negotiations with US President Donald Trump, representing Canada's biggest trading partner, Carney said that he and his compatriots had come to realize the country was too dependent on the economic powerhouse to the south.

"The lesson we've taken, Canadians as a whole, is we're overdependent on the United States. Too closely connected to the United States. And we need to build our strength here at home and diversify and deepen our partnerships with like-minded countries internationally," Carney said.
Canada is too reliant on the United States, Carney tells DW
What did Carney say about EU talks and closer ties to the bloc?
An EU delegation led by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa held talks with Carney and other Canadian officials in Montreal on Friday.

They're discussing the plans floated by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to forge what she called an "associate membership" — a status that does not yet exist for any other country — even as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government resists creating this label. Carney seemed to speak in its favor.

"Well, I think the advantage of what we're doing is that a few things are absolutely clear, irrespective of the exact terminology that's used. President von der Leyen uses associated membership. We use associated membership," he told DW's Katharina Kroll at Port of Montreal Tower.

"What does that mean? It means the closest possible partnership without being a full member of the European Union, because Canada is not in Europe geographically and therefore cannot have accession." Carney said.

blocks.caption: Carney and EU leaders met at an EU-Canada summit in Montreal this weekImage: Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What scope for EU-Canada cooperation does Carney see?

Asked if he was looking to create a "new transatlantic bloc without the US," Carney said it was more about diversifying and deepening Canada's other partnerships than excluding by far its largest trading partner.

"We're both partners of the United States, obviously close partners, alliance partners in NATO. And there are many, many opportunities for cooperation with the United States," he said. "But in many cases, there'll be much deeper cooperation for Canada between Canada and Europe than Canada and the United States."

He mentioned both existing areas of cooperation like the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), calling it "one of the most successful free trade agreements in the world," and also pointed to research cooperation and programs like Horizon Europe and Erasmus+ enabling student exchanges.
But Carney also pointed to areas where the two sides could seek to expand cooperation, naming areas like space technologies, artificial intelligence and critical minerals.

blocks.caption: Carney said that, like von der Leyen but possibly unlike Germany's Friedrich Merz, he uses the term associate membership to describe the status Canada seeksImage: Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Is Canada concerned the talks could alienate the US, or Trump?

Despite his well-documented difficulties with Donald Trump — perhaps most crudely exemplified by Trump's attempts to unilaterally rename Lake Ontario, or his posting AI videos imagining him as an ice hockey player beating Carney up in a fight — Carney said US-Canadian ties were too deep to be derailed by any governments or prime ministers or presidents.

"The bonds between Canadians and Americans are longstanding. They're very strong. And big elements of that will be maintained regardless of the government in Canada, the government in the United States, the combination of the two," he said.

Asked about the best way to deal with Trump, Carney said it was "to be direct, to be clear, to be absolutely clear about your bottom lines are." He said it was important to show respect but also to continue to bring "the negotiations back to the core issues."
But he said the tensions with Trump had demonstrated the need to diversify and to seek Canada's other most natural partners around the world.

blocks.caption: Carney has been in the midst of difficult trade talks with Donald Trump, who has at times shown his dissatisfaction with his neighbor to the north as only he can Image: Dmytro Rusanov/DW

blocks.text: He acknowledged that no matter the nature of the talks with the EU, "the scale of the relationship with the United States" would be "very hard to replace."
Asked if he was concerned that the talks could expose him to further tariffs or other punitive measures from the Trump administration, Carney said, "We've been living with this for some time."
"There have been many justifications for trade action against Canada that the United States has had," he said. "Our view is that all of them are unjustified under our trade agreement."

Carney said the crucial message, also for the Trump White House, was that the talks with Brussels concerned a "positive association" and partnership "to help solve global problems" and address global challenges.
"It's not against somebody. It's for. It's a positive act," he said.
Are the EU and Canada moving closer?
DW's Katharina Kroll conducted the interview in Montreal.

articles.title: Police deployed during stand-off over control of Poland's top court
articles.summary: It comes after the government suspended two senior justices and moved to bring criminal charges against them.

blocks.text: In a social media post, the Constitutional Tribunal wrote that the two men were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.
"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said his government was acting to restore the rule of law.

In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."
President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, ordered his plane be turned back to Warsaw on his way to Senegal to attend the Summer Youth Olympic Games.
The Constitutional Tribunal was the spark that triggered Poland's long-running rule of law dispute after the PiS-led government took office in 2015.
The PiS majority in parliament quickly moved to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.

Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.

The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Tribunal was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.

Taking office in 2023, Tusk vowed to depoliticise the judiciary - but he has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.
Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Tribunal judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.
One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.
Earlier this month, the Council of Europe's advisory body on constitutional matters, the Venice Commission, said Nawrocki should swear-in the judges to allow them to sit on the court's bench.
Żurek said Święczkowski and his vice-president should face criminal charges for not allowing the judges to adjudicate.
Some of Tusk's supporters have accused him of failing to act decisively to reverse the PiS-era reforms.
Parliamentary elections are scheduled next year, and some see his move as an attempt to boost Tusk's popularity among those voters.
But his actions have been criticised. In September, Tusk put forward a politician, Maciej Berek, a lawyer who served as a minister in his cabinet, as a judge candidate to the court.

Lawyer Marcin Matczak, a critic of the PiS-era judicial reform who has stated he considers Święczkowski to be the court's worst president, said his suspension had no legal basis "for a million reasons".
"Today's action at the Constitutional Tribunal, in my opinion, buries this body and the issue of the rule of law for two decades," Prof Matczak wrote on social media.

"Images of armed police and legal interpretations according to which the minister of justice can remove the president of the Constitutional Tribunal by decree will have a powerful, anti-rule of law backlash for years to come," he added.

articles.title: Montreal police chief defends push to change force's culture, weed out bad apples
articles.summary: As accusations of misconduct against Montreal’s police service mount, Chief Fady Dagher says he is taking concrete steps to bring change from the ground up while investigating and potentially…

image.caption: Montreal police Chief Fady Dagher says efforts have been made to weed out the 1% of police officers who deliberately tarnish the uniform. (CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal

As accusations of misconduct against Montreal’s police service mount, Chief Fady Dagher says he is taking concrete steps to bring change from the ground up while investigating and potentially prosecuting those "one per cent" of officers who "tarnish the uniform."
Chief Dagher says more information will be released next month
This comes after new allegations arose at Station 39 in Montréal-Nord, which has been at the centre of a major racism scandal since June.
Now, the Quebec Crown prosecution's office is investigating an officer who, according to Radio-Canada sources, allegedly deleted evidence from a victim's phone in a case of domestic violence in 2025.
Also in recent news, Quebec's domestic security minister has ordered two separate investigations into a Montreal police officer who allegedly urinated on homeless people while in uniform.

But the latest claims are not the first time the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) has faced accusations of misconduct, having been the subject of serious allegations of police brutality and discrimination in the past.

In a news conference Friday, Dagher insisted he has been working tirelessly to not only weed out those on the force who are breaking laws and policies, but also prevent more such officers from being hired.
"We have reviewed everything," Dagher said, citing recruitment, training and promotion processes. "It didn’t happen in a day. It took several years, and believe me, it’s not over."

items: Montreal police officer allegedly deleted domestic violence evidence from victim's phone

blocks.text: The SPVM, he said, has overhauled the internal investigative norms and standards. Dagher said the police service also put tools in place so officers can flag their colleagues for misconduct, and "the 99 per cent responded" by reporting those who break protocol or the law.
The majority of officers, he explained, do admirable work, day after day, risking their lives to protect others.
"I have always told my police officers since I was hired that I would always defend them in the context of their work during emergency responses," he said, noting mistakes are inevitable.
"But I say again today, that I will be merciless to those who intentionally and deliberately conduct themselves in a way that tarnishes the uniform."

He defended his actions back in June when a 16-member patrol unit from Station 39 was suspended following allegations of discrimination and misconduct. More suspensions followed as the investigation continued in the weeks and months since.

items: Did a lack of veteran oversight set the stage for a Montreal police scandal?

blocks.text: Some question why he didn’t fire these officers immediately, he said, but "I wanted to do more." That includes a thorough investigation into not just the individuals, but any potential accomplices.
"And an investigation of this kind takes time," he said. He acknowledged that many people are impatient, especially the victims, who have been "waiting too long."
He said more information will be released in November.

items: Montreal police allegedly cut locs from people's hair. Here's the anti-Black history behind that

blocks.text: Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada has come out in support of Dagher, saying she is confident in his effort to bring cultural change to the SPVM and rid the service of "bad apples."
"I think we have someone who wants to tackle this culture. So, let's give him the chance to do that," she said.
"Let's give him the chance to speak to the citizens and strengthen their sense of security towards their police service."
Dagher was promoted to the role of police chief in November 2022.

items: Montreal approves motion — with amendments — for police chief to appear before council

blocks.text: Opposition Leader Ericka Alneus said the most recent allegations "shatter the confidence of people in vulnerable situations who need to feel that society is behind them."
She said the mayor "must take responsibility, show leadership and summon the police chief to an extraordinary city council meeting to answer public questions."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Isaac Olson is a journalist with CBC Montreal. He worked largely as a newspaper reporter and photographer for 15 years before joining CBC in the spring of 2018.
With files from Radio-Canada

articles.title: Ukraine: Oleshky residents evacuate war-ravaged city
articles.summary: Under the local ceasefire, an aid convoy of 25 buses arrived with humanitarian aid and as transport for fleeing Oleshky residents. The Ukrainian city has been occupied by Russia since 2022 and faces…

image.caption: The Red Cross is on the ground in Oleshky assisting residentsImage: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Residents of Russian-occupied Oleshky, in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, evacuated the war-torn city on Friday.
The evacuations come in the fourth day of a ceasefire in the city, the most significant truce since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine over four years ago.
The local ceasefire was brokered by US first lady Melania Trump. Pope Leo XIV also participated in deliberations with Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
Under the ceasefire deal, an aid convoy of 25 buses, some ambulances, trucks and other vehicles arrived in the city earlier on Friday to deliver food and medicine to residents.
Demining operations preceeded the aid convoy's arrival, with a Russian sapper and one other person killed in the process.
Officials from both Ukraine and Russia came to gether in the rare joint humanitarian effort, which is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
How did the evacuations take place?

According to the plan, an estimated 2,000 remaining Oleshky residents were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian-held territory, Russian-held territory, or to remain in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

If residents chose to go to Ukraine, they would travel 450 kilometers (280 miles) through Russian-held Crimea to reach the city of Anapa in southern Russia. Then they would fly to Belarus before crossing the border into northern Ukraine.
Russia's lead representative on the mission, Yana Lantratova, said buses would transport residents who want to live in Russia.
It remained unclear how many people chose to leave the city, but Melania Trump posted on social media that the convoy had safely evacuated more than 750 people.
Aid convoy reaches frontline town of Oleshky
Harrowing conditions
Oleshky residents have spoken of the harrowing conditions they have had to suffer in the city, such as traveling along mine-strewn roads in search for food and water.
"The problem is that a lot of people are staying," one woman told Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets.
"I've been told that it's their own choice," Lubinets replied. "At the very least, we'll do what we can to ensure that somehow humanitarian aid gets through."
Lubinets was in charge of coordinating the operation with Lantratova.
The pair appeared side by side to address reporters and were cordial to one another, something not seen between Russian and Ukrainian officials since the start of the war.

articles.title: Feds tap Delta, B.C., port expansion as 'project of national interest'
articles.summary: The federal government has listed Roberts Bank Terminal 2 in Delta, B.C., as a "project of national interest" to expand and diversify Canada's trade capacity.

image.caption: Roberts Bank Terminal is seen from Delta, B.C., on Wednesday, Jan. 22, 2025. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
The federal government has listed Roberts Bank Terminal 2 in Delta, B.C., as a "project of national interest" to expand and diversify Canada's trade capacity.
Project expected to add 2.4 million containers of annual capacity at Port of Vancouver

In a news release, the government said the listing will give the project the "immediate regulatory certainty" it needs to be built at the Port of Vancouver, while keeping environmental safeguards and holding consultation with Indigenous communities.
The project, which is a proposed three-berth container terminal at Roberts Bank, will be led by the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority.
A final investment decision is expected by mid-2027, according to the release.
The national interest designation, the release says, "accelerates the project's commercial operations by up to four years, from 2039 to 2035."

items: Federal government refers Port of Vancouver strategy to Major Projects Office

blocks.text: The Roberts Bank Terminal 2 project is expected to add 2.4 million containers of annual capacity at the port, increasing container capacity at the Port of Vancouver by about 50 per cent.
The government said the project will support about 17,000 jobs across Canada's supply chains and contribute about $3 billion annually to the national GDP.
The port authority has selected TerraMarine as its preferred construction partner after a competitive procurement process.
